title: 조엘 델링거: 두 주인을 섬길 수 없습니다 (마태 6:24)

en.text: The theme I would like to address
this morning is
“Guard Against Materialism.”
And I invite you to take
another look at our day’s text
at Matthew 6:24.
Here couched in the Sermon on the Mount,
Jesus addressed his disciples and the crowds
with an all-inclusive truth.
Notice how that verse begins:
“No one can slave for two masters.”
Are there any exceptions to that rule?
According to Jesus, according to Jehovah God,
no—no exceptions.
But who are the two competing and very different masters
that Jesus was referring to?
The end of the verse answers
where he refers to “God” and “Riches.”
Did you notice that “Riches” is presented here in the Bible
with a capital “R” to begin?
Now, that’s interesting when we notice Jesus’ other references to riches
in the New World Translation where the “r” is not capitalized
—lowercase “riches.”
For example, when Jesus refers later
to the deceptive power of riches
that can choke the word, lowercase “r.”
Or when he referred to unrighteous riches
that we need to use wisely, lowercase “r.”
So why, here at Matthew 6:24
and in the parallel account at Luke 16:13,
did the New World Bible Translation Committee
choose to capitalize the “R”?
Well, the study edition of the New World Translation helps us here.
It tells us at Matthew 6:24
that the Greek word used here is traditionally translated “Mammon”
—that could also be rendered as “Riches” or “Money.”
And then the comment adds this gem:
It says that in this verse
‘“Riches” is personified as a master,
or a kind of false god.’
Well, we’ve seen that to be true, haven’t we?
For generations humans have tended to elevate riches:
good old money, riches —lowercase “m” and lowercase “r.”
And they’ve elevated it to be a god that has,
as our commenters commented on, enslaved millions.
What was the teaching Jesus was highlighting for his followers?
It’s that we —Christians—
cannot give God the exclusive devotion that he deserves
and at the same time be devoted to gathering up more material possessions.
That’s a very strong warning.
So that leads us to two questions that we could consider
with the balance of our time this morning:
What is materialism?
And how can you and I guard against falling into that snare
of gathering up more riches
and making this our god?
Merriam-Webster’s Dictionary offers this definition of materialism:
It’s “a preoccupation with [or a tendency to seek after]
“or stress upon material [things]
rather than intellectual or spiritual things.”
But I found a definition in the publications of the faithful slave
that I think is even better for all of us in the context of Jesus’ words.
The 1978 Yearbook, on page 9, expressed it this way:
“It has been said that materialism is anything
“that stands between a person and his worship of Jehovah.
“So it need not necessarily be an expensive automobile,
“an ostentatious home or a large bank account.
“It could be anything that absorbs a person’s time and attention
so that he neglects the worship due to Jehovah.”
Well, that’s the point, isn’t it, that Jesus was trying
to stress for his followers?
Could materialism entrap any of us
who have chosen to put Kingdom interests first
and have made material sacrifices in order to do that?
Well, that question prompted me to think of a faithful servant of Jehovah
outlined in the Bible book of Jeremiah —Baruch.
Open, please, to Jeremiah chapter 45.
Now, as we think about the faithful servant Jeremiah
and his secretary, Baruch,
we can imagine that they made considerable sacrifices
to serve the interests of Jehovah’s people at that time.
Baruch had a special privilege of service,
as do most of us here today,
but something distracted him.
Notice, please, the reading at Jeremiah 45:3.
Here Jehovah pinpointed what Baruch had said,
perhaps only in his heart, only in his own thoughts.
Verse 3: “You have said:
“‘Woe to me, for Jehovah has added grief to my pain!
I am weary from my groaning, and I have found no resting-place.’”
Baruch was tired.
He’d been serving Jehovah faithfully,
but his assignment was difficult, perhaps stressful.
And it was going to be 18 more years until the foretold destruction would come.
But was it his service to Jehovah that was really the problem?
Notice what Jehovah identified, as we read verse 5:
“But you are seeking great things for yourself.
Stop seeking such things.”
Those “great things” could have been material things.
It could have been that he was ensnared by materialism.
If that was the case,
Jehovah’s warning to stop seeking such things was timely.
Later on in that same verse, Baruch was reminded that his life
—not his possessions, not his things—
was going to be the spoil that Jehovah was going to provide
at the upcoming destruction.
Well, how can we guard against falling into the snare of materialism?
Like Baruch, we from time to time need to take a long hard look
at our personal view of money and personal things.
The September 2015 issue of the Awake! magazine
posed some questions for self-examination.
Here are just a few of them:
“Am I attracted to get-rich-quick schemes?
“Do I find it difficult to be generous with my money?
“Does money make me feel important?
“Am I always thinking about money?
“Is my attitude toward money
adversely affecting my health and family life?”
You know, real-life experiences among our brothers and sisters
prove that we all need to be thinking seriously about this matter.
Alex, one of our brothers, got caught up in trading in the stock market,
thinking he could soon quit his job and enter the pioneer service.
He was well-motivated,
but he got caught in a vortex
of studying offers and market reports.
He used his savings and money borrowed from brokers
to buy stocks that the analysts
had predicted would quickly rise in value.
Do you know how the story plays out for Alex?
Months passed, the stocks never rebounded.
Alex lost his savings and ended up having to sell his home.
What a painful consequence
of being deceived by this cruel master —money.
Alex reflected on what took place, and he said this:
“I caused my family great pain.
“I now know that anyone who puts his trust in Satan’s system
will be profoundly disappointed.”
There was another experience of a Sister Valentine from Jamaica
that caught my attention when I was researching this point.
You may remember the article that was published
in the January 1, 2006, issue of The Watchtower,
“Bringing Up Eight Children in Jehovah’s Ways Was a Challenge and a Joy.”
Our sister related an experience that involved her view of material things.
Now, we keep in mind that she was not well-to-do financially.
Imagine, a mother of eight —the husband has abandoned her—
she’s raising them to serve Jehovah.
But does the fact that we may have a little, financially speaking,
mean that we’re immune to the trap of materialism?
In 1988, Hurricane Gilbert devastated the island.
She wrote this:
“We left our home for shelter in a safer place.
“During a lull in the storm, my son and I left the refuge area
“to survey the wreckage that was once our home.
“While poking around in the debris, I spotted something I wanted to save.
“Suddenly, winds were howling again,
but I still held on to what I had salvaged.”
Her son spoke up, “Mom, put down the television.
Are you Lot’s wife?”
Our sister commented that that comment from her son
caught her and returned her to her senses.
She dropped the rain-soaked TV, and they ran for safety.
Sister Valentine did a self-examination.
She thought about what took place at that moment.
She says: “I recall that I risked my life for a TV.”
But it warmed her heart that her son had the spiritual insight
to provide her a warning at the right time.
Well, it’s a good lesson for all of us, isn’t it?
No matter what our economic situation may be,
we need to view money as a skillful tool
and use it for that purpose,
but not allow it to rule or control us.
We do not want to ‘stab ourselves all over with many pains.’

cn.text: 我今天要讲的主题是
提防物质主义
想请你们再看看今天的经文
马太福音6:24
这是耶稣在登山宝训中
对门徒和群众说的
这句话适用于所有人
留意经文开头说
“一个人不能做两个主人的奴隶”
真的不能事奉两个主人吗?
在耶稣和耶和华看来
答案是  不能
耶稣说的
互相对立的两个主人
是指谁呢?
经文的后面告诉我们
是上帝和财富
在英语圣经中
这里的“财富”用了
大写的首字母“R”
有意思的是
在《圣经新世界译本》中
耶稣在其他地方提及财富时
经文用的是小写的“r”
例如  耶稣提及骗人的财富
可以挤死上帝的话语时
经文是小写的“r”
他提到要善用不义的钱财时
“钱财”的首字母也是小写的
可是马太福音6:24和相关经文
路加福音16:13里
经文中  “财富”一词的首字母
都用大写的“R”
为什么呢?
《精读本圣经》给我们做了一个解释
马太福音6:24里的
“财富”这个词的希腊语原文
一般译作“玛门”
也就是金钱或钱财的意思
精读本的解释也说
这节经文中的财富被拟人化了
被比作一个主人或者假神
这个说法很贴切  对吗?
自古以来  很多人都尊崇财富
追求财富
把财富当神一样看待
财富的确成了神
成了主人
就像之前弟兄评论的一样
已经有无数的人成为了它的奴隶
所以耶稣在这里强调的要点是什么呢?
就是我们基督徒
如果总想着为自己积攒财富
就不可能全心全意地崇拜上帝
这是个很严厉的警告
接下来我们一起考虑以下两个问题
物质主义是什么?
我们怎样才能避免
陷入物质主义的网罗
不把财富当作自己的神?
《韦氏词典》给物质主义
下的定义是这样的
倾向于或实际上
全心沉迷于满足物质需求和欲望
完全忽视信仰和精神层面的追求
我在忠信睿智奴隶出版的刊物里
找到了另一个解释
也许能帮助我们
更好地明白耶稣的意思
1978年的英语年鉴第9页这样说
“任何妨碍我们专心崇拜耶和华的东西”
“都可能让人落入物质主义的陷阱”
“这些东西不仅仅是名车”
“豪宅或巨额存款”
“凡是占据人的时间  精力的东西”
“都有可能影响人崇拜耶和华”
的确是这样
这就是耶稣想强调的要点  对吗?
我们已经在追求王国
也为了王国在物质方面做出了牺牲
但我们也有可能
陷入物质主义的陷阱吗?
这个问题让我想到
耶利米书中的一个忠仆
那就是巴录
请打开耶利米书45章
请考虑一下上帝的忠仆耶利米
和他的书记巴录
他们当时为了帮助上帝的子民
肯定做出了很多牺牲
就像今天在座的许多人一样
巴录有一个特别的服务机会
但是他却因为一些事情分心了
请读一下耶利米书45:3
巴录的话很可能
只是他內心的想法
没有说出来
耶和华却看出了他心里的想法
第3节说
“你说  我有祸了!”
“我痛苦不堪”
“耶和华还给我加上悲痛”
“我呻吟叹息”
“疲乏困顿  无法安歇”
巴录非常疲惫
他一直忠心事奉耶和华
而且他的委派很不容易
这也许让他很有压力
另外  当时距离耶路撒冷的毁灭
还有18年的时间
但是问题在于他的委派吗?
请注意耶和华在第5节怎么说
“你还为自己图谋大事吗?”
“不要图谋了”
巴录图谋的“大事”
很可能是物质财富
他可能陷入了物质主义的陷阱
耶和华给他的警告很适时
因为要真是这样
巴录会很危险
经文后面说耶和华提醒巴录
在毁灭来到时
他要保护的是巴录的性命
而不是他的财富
或他拥有的东西
可以怎么避免跌入同样的陷阱呢?
我们像巴录一样
也需要常常省察自己
对物质财富的看法
2015年9月的《警醒!》杂志
列出了一些
帮我们自我省察的问题
例如
“我对那些高风险的投资计划”
“是不是很感兴趣呢?”
“我很不愿意为别人付出金钱吗?”
“我拥有的钱财”
“让我觉得自己高人一等吗?”
“我总是想着钱吗?”
“我对金钱的观念”
“是不是影响我的健康”
“和家庭生活呢?”
弟兄姐妹的经历也说明
我们所有人都需要认真考虑这个问题
一个叫亚历克斯的弟兄
迷上了股票买卖
他以为很快就能赚到钱
就能辞掉工作开始做先驱了
他的动机很好
但他需要花很多精力
去了解股票和市场行情
他听信了经济专家的话
用自己的积蓄
买了据说有升值潜力的股票
甚至还向别人借了钱
结果怎么样呢?
几个月过去了
股票一直没有上涨
亚历克斯花光了全部积蓄
甚至卖掉了自己的房子
被财富这个冷酷无情的主人欺骗
后果多么可悲!
亚历克斯回想自己的经历后说
我为家人带来很大的痛苦
现在我知道
谁信赖撒但的制度
谁的希望就一定会破灭
还有一个经历
是关于瓦伦丁姐妹的
她来自牙买加
我准备演讲的时候
特别留意到她的经历
2006年1月1日《守望台》的一篇文章
题目是
《按照耶和华的意思抚养八个儿女 ——经历艰苦  却满心喜乐》
这位姐妹在讲述自己经历时
提到了她对物质财富的看法
请留意她并不是一个富裕的人
她被丈夫拋弃了
还要抚养八个孩子
教导他们事奉耶和华
如果我们跟她经济状况差不多
是不是就不可能
落入物质主义的陷阱呢?
1988年飓风吉尔伯特侵袭了牙买加
姐妹写道
我们离开家
到安全的地方避难
风暴稍微平静时
我和儿子回去看我们的房子
在坍塌的废墟里
我发现了一个东西
于是我抱起来想带走
突然又刮起狂风
我还是抱着那个东西不放
这时她的儿子说
妈妈  把电视扔了!
别做罗得的妻子啊!
听到儿子的话
这位姐妹顿时醒悟过来
她扔下湿漉漉的电视机
逃到了安全的地方
瓦伦丁姐妹在事后自我省察
她回想当时的情况说
为了一个电视机
我竟然不顾自己的生命!
但她的儿子在危急时刻提醒了她
这让她感到很欣慰
这给我们上了宝贵的一课  对吗?
不论我们的经济情况怎样
我们都要对钱财有合理的看法
财物不过是我们手上的工具
我们要控制它  善用它
而不是被它控制
我们绝不想
“用许多痛苦把自己刺得遍体鳞伤”

en.text: As we tell about the Kingdom, As we witness for your name,
There are many who oppose us And who try to bring us shame.
But instead of fearing men, It’s really you we must obey.
So we beg you now for your spirit; O Jehovah, hear what we pray.
Grant us boldness as we witness; Help us overcome our fear.
Give us confidence and courage So that all the world may hear.
Armageddon draws ever near, But until that great day is here,
Grant us boldness as we witness. This is our prayer.
Even though we may be fearful, You remember we are dust.
Your assurance to support us Is a promise we can trust.
Give attention to the threats Of those who persecute and blame.
May you help us all to continue As we boldly speak in your name.
Grant us boldness as we witness; Help us overcome our fear.
Give us confidence and courage So that all the world may hear.
Armageddon draws ever near, But until that great day is here,
Grant us boldness as we witness. This is our prayer.

en.text: The next part is a video entitled The Inside Story,
hosted by Brother Ken Stovall,
who also serves as a Theocratic Schools instructor.
I am so excited to be with you here again
on this segment of The Inside Story!
This time we’re with class number 143 of the Gilead School,
and you are going to meet some adorable brothers and sisters.
And let me tell you,
they have some moving experiences to relate to you.
And we’re going to solve two fascinating mysteries.
And we have music.
Students in this class are going
to thrill you with their musical talent.
There is a captivating song that they’re going to sing for you.
So come with me as we, together,
get “the inside story.”
Let’s introduce our first guest.
And that would be Saša Komaromi from the Serbia branch.
So, Brother Komaromi, you serve at the Serbia branch.
But you told me that some years ago, before you were in the truth,
you discovered that there were two main interests you had in life.
One of them had to do with a career choice.
Could you explain that?
One was music.
Music.
Now, is this a picture of you?
That was the old me.
Evidently, you were in a band.
Yes, we were at a competition at the time.
That was one of your interests, but there was another.
What was that?
Searching for the purpose of life.
And how did you go about searching for life’s purpose?
I read a lot of books
—books about parapsychology, Buddhism,
spiritism, Tibetan Lamaism.
Amazing! That’s a lot of books.
Now, at the time, though, you were dating your wife, Vicki.
What did she think of all these books?
Did she share your interest in all this reading?
I wished she did.
But no, she did not.
To be honest, it’s not really easy
to like to read those kinds of books
—for example, The Book of the Dead.
The Book of the Dead?
I can see that’s not going to be a very enjoyable book.
Now, was it only books?
Was that the only way you were searching for the purpose of life?
No, I was also experimenting with different states of mind
under the influence of drugs.
During my hallucinations,
I had many things already “solved.”
You had everything “solved.”
This is what I thought.
But after I came to myself again,
I was again in the same room and everything was the same.
So I was really, really disappointed.
And then I prayed to God.
I said: “God, I’m asking just for one thing.
But whatever it is, just, please, help me to be certain that I find the truth.”
Very interesting.
So you prayed for Jehovah to help you find the truth.
Of course, you didn’t know Jehovah at the time.
So how was your prayer answered?
Soon after that, I went to Germany.
I had the idea to form my music studio.
During my visit there,
I understood that my uncle and my aunt were Jehovah’s Witnesses.
And you never knew that before?
No. No, I didn’t know.
So, what did they have in their home that would have been really exciting to you?
As all Jehovah’s Witnesses, they had a lot of theocratic books.
Ahh.
So, did you read the books?
Yes, I read them a lot.
Actually, I read a book daily.
Wow!
So you get back home; you open up the suitcases.
And Vicki is there, and she sees books.
And you were supposed to bring home musical equipment.
What did she think about that?
She thought, ‘Now definitely he’s totally crazy.’
So, what did you do?
I explained to her immediately that from now on
I would like to live according to what I read in these books and the Bible.
And I would also like it for her —that she also live like that.
If this was OK with her, we could stay together.
If it was not OK with her, we were finished.
You like to be direct, don’t you?
I know, I was “very tactful.”
But I also offered her the book Young People Ask.
Did she like that?
Yes.
Yes, she liked it much more than my ultimatum.
I see.
We started studying the Bible.
At the beginning, my wife started because of me,
but later she did this because of herself.
And after six months, we became unbaptized publishers.
Then we got married, and we were baptized in 1994.
Immediately, we started full-time service,
and we served five years as regular pioneers
and then almost five years as special pioneers.
And now we’ve been 13 years at the Serbia branch.
Jehovah has answered your prayer.
You’re satisfied;
you found the truth; you found the purpose in life.
But there’s still the music.
Did you have to give up your desire to play music,
to be involved in music, especially since you’ve come to Bethel now?
Actually, in 2013,
there was an idea that we should start with a project
of recording vocal renditions of our theocratic songs.
And my wife, Violeta, and I had the privilege to participate in that project.
Now, was this just for the Serbia branch?
No, the plan was to record the songs in four or five languages.
Four or five languages?
But would this mean, then, that you would travel
around to different countries surrounding Serbia?
No, the idea was that singers
would come from other countries to Serbia,
and they would be full-time singers
for a period of time until we finished that project.
That must have been a tremendous amount of work.
How did you get that accomplished?
Yeah, it’s easier if we see a video,
and it will be much more understandable.
All right, good. Let’s watch the video.
One of the first things we needed was a recording studio.
So with the help of many, we built our own.
A typical day began with a little music theory,
a little stretching,
and a brief review of the song’s Scriptural theme.
Once they received a new song,
they practiced in separate groups.
Then they would all come together.
Finally, it was time to record.
This resulted in 450 songs being recorded
in a period of 22 months.
Looking back, these songs were sung not just with words
but with hearts full of love for Jehovah.
Look at them.
Those are nice greetings at the end there.
Yeah, nice surprise.
I loved the way the chorus sounded.
You did a good job with them.
That must have been a tremendous amount of work,
getting that all done, though, in five different languages.
Yes, the singers did a great job and also all the crew.
And you really could see, all the time,
their love for Jehovah and love for the brotherhood.
And every day you could see a lot of their self-sacrificing spirit.
Now, Saša, let me ask you one more question.
We saw the picture there of you as a musician,
and I know you have some musical talent.
Possibly, you could have become famous.
Do you ever regret not pursuing some sort of a career in the world
as opposed to giving your life in full-time service to Jehovah?
As you said, I could be famous.
Or I could have become a drug addict and now be dead.
That’s a good point.
So no, no regrets at all.
I received much, much more than I ever imagined.
And in my case, from my first prayer till now,
Jehovah assured me that he’s really the “Hearer of prayer,”
as the psalmist mentioned in Psalm 65:2.
Excellent! Thank you so much, Saša,
for sharing these very heartfelt comments.
You’re welcome.
Thank you.
Now, you know what we’re going to do?
We’re going to give you the opportunity
to get to know some of the students
in our audience.
We’re going to do an activity
I call What’s My Favorite Scripture?
So we’re going to ask the students if they’ll volunteer
and give us their favorite scripture and, in a minute or less,
tell us what it says and why it’s their favorite scripture.
OK,
let’s see now.
Who would like to go first?
Shingirai Mapfumo from Zimbabwe.
Psalm 84:11.
And what does that say?
“For Jehovah God is a sun and a shield;
“he gives favor and glory.
“Jehovah will not hold back anything good
from those walking in integrity.”
OK, so tell us, Why is that your favorite scripture?
During the economic crisis in Zimbabwe,
my pioneer partner and I ran out of food.
We were really starving,
and physically we were so weak that we could not even function.
Still, we managed to go to town,
hoping that we could get some money from the bank.
There was a long queue,
and the bank was not giving any money either.
We were so distraught.
At that moment when we didn’t know what to do,
a truck from the branch office brought food supplies for us.
Then it became so clear to me
that Jehovah is “a shield,”
and he never “hold[s] back anything good” from his loyal servants.
Amazing! Well, I can see why that’s your favorite scripture.
All right, who else?
Let’s get Sister Tšèpang Mhlongo,
and she’s from South Africa.
My favorite scripture is Psalm 68:5,
and it says about Jehovah
that he is the “father of the fatherless and a protector of widows.”
Why is that your favorite scripture?
Well, I became motherless when I was only one year old.
But Jehovah has provided me with hundreds of mothers around the globe,
both black and white.
And because our Bethel work
involves traveling all around the African continent
working with the translators,
it makes it even more precious to me
that I adopt this family wherever we go.
Truly, Jehovah has proved to be my Father
and my Protector to this day.
Hmm, very touching.
And I’m sure that all of those parents who have adopted you
are proud to have you as a daughter.
Who else could tell us their favorite scripture?
All right, let’s get Brother Sylvain Bois from Benin.
It is Psalm 94:18, 19.
And what does it say?
“Your loyal love, O Jehovah, kept supporting me.
“When anxieties overwhelmed me,
you comforted and soothed me.”
So tell us, Why is that scripture special to you?
Years ago, when I was attending Ministerial Training School (MTS),
I had a serious stroke and I was hospitalized.
When I awoke from the coma,
I felt very happy because I was alive.
But also very discouraged
because I thought everything was over for me
—pioneer service, school,
and even my dream to one day become a missionary.
But one of the instructors and his wife came to the hospital,
and they read me that verse.
And my heart was full of anxieties,
but I really felt that day that Jehovah
was able to comfort me and soothe me.
And you know what?
One year later,
I was permitted to again attend MTS.
And a few months later,
Jehovah fulfilled another of my dreams,
as I was assigned as a missionary in Africa.
Brother Bois, that was very touching.
Thank you so much, and we’re so glad to have you in this class of Gilead.
Well, that’s all that we’re going to have time for.
So now it’s time to introduce our next guest,
and that would be Brother Paulo Maganha, and he’s from Brazil.
Now, Brother Maganha, you’re at the Brazil branch.
But you came into the truth at nine years old,
at the same time as your mother.
And you went to the branch, to Bethel, in your early 20’s,
and you’ve been there for 27 years.
What department do you work in at the branch now?
I am now in LDC for one and a half years.
LDC.
OK, would you just tell us, What does the LDC Department do?
LDC is the Local Design/Construction Department.
It’s responsible for the work of planning,
construction, and maintenance of Kingdom Halls and Assembly Halls.
You have the LDC Department there at Bethel,
but who outside of Bethel
works with building Kingdom Halls and Assembly Halls?
Outside we have many brothers and sisters
serving as construction servants, construction volunteers,
remote volunteers, and field representatives.
Now, this is— This is the mystery.
This is our first mystery.
What really, then, does a field representative do?
OK, let’s just call them field rep. OK?
OK. Field rep, I like that.
You could say that they are the eyes and the ears of the LDC at the branch.
But what if I show you some pictures regarding the work?
I would love that!
OK.
At the first step, the office asks him to investigate some congregation needs.
He meets with the local elders and the circuit overseer
to determine the needs.
And later, he sends a recommendation to the office.
I see. So if he has a large region,
he may have to have many, many of these meetings
and do a lot of research to determine what the needs are for Kingdom Halls.
Yeah.
Once the project is approved,
the next step is to search for appropriate land, a property.
To do that, he goes to the Internet,
consults real estate agents, local brothers, neighbors.
To find the right property at the right cost can be very time consuming
and requires of him a lot of skills and abilities.
And the field rep is also responsible for getting the permits,
the approvals, for construction.
And he visits several different agencies every day
to get the permits to have everything approved by the government.
In big cities, he may have to stand in line after line after line.
This could take—
Yeah. And in bigger cities, it can take even some weeks
or months to get everything approved.
Finally, when everything is approved, the construction group starts the work.
And you can see him again visiting the site
in order to give some technical support to the construction overseer.
So, now, does he stay on the site
when a building is being built?
No, he returns to his office
but remains in contact with the group to give some remote support.
Especially when some big issues arise at the site,
the construction overseer can always count on his good support.
OK, good.
I notice in this picture, behind the field representative,
we see a sister pictured there.
Who might that be?
Well, if he’s married,
his wife can do lots of work to help him.
But if he is not, he can count on a local volunteer to help him.
Once the project is concluded, he visits the site again,
now to do the commissioning
and to make sure that everything was done according to the plans.
So, evidently, his job is done now.
No, not yet.
He’s also responsible for giving training to local brothers
to properly maintain the building.
Wow! So you have helped solve this mystery.
He does have a lot of work to do.
But really, does working on one project keep him busy?
No, it is not just one, Brother Stovall.
They are very busy and productive workers.
On average, each field rep can be working on 10 to 15 projects
in different phases but at the same time.
My goodness! That’s amazing!
So they really do an amazing amount of work then.
Paulo, I understand that at your branch,
you’ve come up with a very innovative idea
regarding Assembly Halls and Kingdom Halls.
Could you explain that to us?
Yes, we have done what is called an expandable Kingdom Hall.
Expandable Kingdom Hall?
Saša, do you have expandable Kingdom Halls in Serbia?
Not that I’m aware of.
I can’t even imagine.
How do you expand a Kingdom Hall?
OK, what if we see a brief video about this?
OK, I’d like that.
At first, it looks like a normal Kingdom Hall.
But something wonderful happens when the back walls are lifted.
It’s now large enough to hold an entire assembly or convention.
But before we can meet there, it has to be cleaned.
Chairs are rented and arranged.
And audio and video equipment must be set up
so that no matter where you sit,
you won’t miss anything.
All the hard work is worth it when you see how much the friends benefit.
When the special weekend of activity is over
and the walls are lowered,
it goes right back to being a Kingdom Hall again.
That’s our family there.
Uh-huh. They sent you some spirited greetings.
Yeah.
And what a brilliant way
to get the most out of a building and save money!
Now, Brother Maganha, I just want to ask you,
What has impressed you the most about working with the LDC Department?
What really touched my heart is to see the spirit of willingness to help
shown by all those involved with the LDC.
You know, these brothers and sisters have left their families,
their houses, their friends behind
to work with these projects.
All these sacrifices are done out of love
—love for our brotherhood and especially love for Jehovah.
That’s the reason that I really, really appreciate their work.
Thank you, Brother Maganha.
Obviously, those brothers and sisters that work with LDC
set a good example for the rest of us.
Thank you very much.
My pleasure.
Now, Brother Komaromi,
it’s time for you to give us a sample of your musical talent.
Would you go and join our band?
Recently, the Governing Body has given us loving encouragement
through our regional convention program to never give up.
Now, the Gilead students have written a song
that goes right along with that spirit and that theme.
It’s entitled “We’ll Never Let Go.”
I thought that was a thrilling song.
You brothers and sisters did a marvelous job on that.
And you know what I liked about the song too
is that it gets progressively more modern
as you go through the song.
So it really says to me that our organization
in its modern-day history,
even in early times, has never given up,
and we will never give up.
And it’s so joyful.
It says that we’re going to endure with joy.
No one can take that away from us.
It’s Jehovah’s gift through his holy spirit.
Now it’s time to introduce our final guest,
and that is Sister Angela Khang from the United States.
Angela, you are one of the single sisters in our class,
but where in the United States do you serve?
I’m at the remote translation office (RTO) in Sacramento, California,
and they translate into the Hmong language there.
Now, I have to confess —the Hmong language—
I never knew until very recently
that there was such a language as the Hmong language.
And I didn’t realize there was a Hmong people.
Why is that?
Well, for a long time, the Hmong story was kept a secret from the American public.
Now this is another one of our mysteries
because why would it be
that someone would try to keep the existence of a whole culture secret?
Well, during the Vietnam War, which was a very unpopular conflict,
many U.S. citizens didn’t want the war to expand.
So the U.S. government actually went to Southeast Asia,
and they secretly recruited the Hmong men
who were living in the hill tribes of Laos
to fight Communism in that part of the world.
In the end, about 40,000 Hmong men were killed in that war,
and so that’s about 1 in 4 Hmong men.
So every family lost someone.
Forty thousand men.
I don’t think that people really are aware of that fact, are they?
No. Many historians call that conflict the Secret War.
Looking at our monitor here, what is it we are seeing here?
This was an exhibit showcasing the Hmong experience
—how they came to the U.S.
And it’s a wall of unknown soldiers who fought in the war,
and they were asking the Hmong community to identify their loved ones.
So a few in our congregation knew some of those men.
I see.
Now, as I think back to the history of that war,
at some point in time, the United States pulled out of Vietnam.
So, what happened then
to the Hmong that were left there in Vietnam when the U.S. pulled out?
It was a desperate situation because there was an aggressive campaign
to capture and kill any of the remaining Hmong families,
and so many of them had to find a way to escape.
And so we see that here in this photo.
This is Long Tieng Air Base in 1975.
About 30,000 Hmong people converged on that airport,
hoping to find a way out.
But only about 2,500 were airlifted —the more prominent officials.
I see.
You can see that those thousands of people there
are not going to fit on that airplane.
So all those thousands that were left behind,
what happened to them?
They were pretty much left on their own,
and they had to find their way out along with thousands of other families.
And so that’s what happened to my family.
They found their way across the Mekong River into Thailand,
and they were placed in refugee camps.
I see.
So who are we seeing a picture of here now on the monitor?
This is my father in a Thailand refugee camp
and my mother, my grandmother, and my uncle.
So your family managed to survive by fleeing into Thailand
and getting into the refugee camp.
But then how did they get to the United States?
In 1979, they were sponsored to the United States.
And the Hmong culture is patriarchal, so you stick close with your clan.
And so my entire clan ended up in California, and they settled in South Sacramento.
I can imagine that this experience must have been a tremendous amount of loss
for the Hmong people, Hmong families.
My father lost his mother when they were fleeing;
he lost his brother.
He saw many people lose their lives.
Many clans were separated.
Some of their relatives ended up in France,
and the rest of them ended up in the United States.
And then when they settled here, my mom lost her hearing.
So it was just an added stress in their lives.
So how did all this suffering and loss, how did it affect your mother?
Even though her background is animist,
she knew that the Bible was a holy book that would teach her about the Creator.
So she found comfort in reading the Bible.
And she started to collect different Bibles from different translations
and comparing them to try to understand what she was reading.
And every night she would pray with me and my sister.
And so from a young age, we were taught that God is real,
even though we didn’t know Jehovah yet.
Wow, very, very interesting.
So she was really, really looking for the truth.
So how did she eventually find the truth?
Well, in the meantime, my uncle (the one who was pictured earlier)
and his wife started studying the Bible, and they came into the truth.
And they asked a sister to come and study with my mom,
and soon my entire family was studying.
In 1996, my mom was baptized.
In 1997, my sister and I were baptized.
Amazing! So, now, you were baptized at the age of 12,
and then you started pioneering at the age of 15.
Yes.
Now, first of all, you were in an English congregation.
But what changed that?
Our circuit overseer came through, and he was telling us about a Hmong group
that had formed in our sister congregation.
And he told us we had no reason to be in English,
and he was right.
So as a family, we moved over to the Hmong group,
and in 1999, that group became the very first Hmong congregation.
So that made us very happy.
So you were associated with the very first Hmong congregation
anywhere in the world.
Yes.
Amazing!
Now, later you toured Bethel, and that had a profound effect on you.
Can you tell us about that?
Well, we came to Bethel, and a brother in Translation Services
found out we were coming through, so he wanted to meet with us.
And he sat us girls down, and he told us,
“You have something you can give to Jehovah, and that’s your language.”
So it really got me thinking
about what I could do to really support the field.
So I went home, and I really worked on my language
and worked on supporting the group.
And in 2007
when Bethel came looking for translators,
this same brother came out and he interviewed a group of us.
And shortly after that, my mom and another brother and I
were invited to serve on the Hmong translation team
at the first RTO here in the U.S. branch.
My goodness!
So the first Hmong congregation anywhere in the world
and the first RTO for the U.S. branch.
Jehovah certainly has blessed you with some wonderful privileges.
Could you just tell us,
What’s it like working at the RTO from day to day?
Sure. Would you like to see a video?
Yes, we would.
At the Hmong RTO, many hands help in the translation work.
When questions come up, we’re not left on our own.
The Translation Services Department is always ready to provide support.
Once everything is approved, it’s time to record.
Since Hmong wasn’t a written language until the 1950’s,
audio publications are very important to the Hmong field.
Some support the RTO in other valuable ways too,
such as cooking and cleaning.

title: 술을 마시기 전에 어떤 점을 생각해 보아야 할까?

ko.text: 즐거운 시간을 보낼 수 있다고 생각해.
술이 “뱀처럼 물” 수 있다고 알려 줘.
청소년이 술 마시는 걸 금지하는 곳에 살고 있니?
그런데도 술을 마시면 벌금을 내야 할 수도 있고
사회봉사 활동을 하게 될 수도 있고
술을 마시면 자제력이 약해져서 문제를 겪을 수 있어.
나중에 후회할 말이나 행동을 하게 될 수 있지.
어떤 애들이 술을 마시기 시작하면 어떡하지?
성경은 지혜로운 사람은 문제가 생기려고 할 때
그 자리에 계속 있으면 어떤 일이 생길까?
문제가 생기기 전에 어떻게 거길 떠날 수 있을까?
부모님께 데리러 와 달라는 전화나 문자를 하겠다고
다른 사람이 하라는 대로 하는 사람은
그 사람의 종이 되는 거나 마찬가지라고 알려 주지.
친구들이 하는 대로 무작정 따라 하면
친구들이 원하는 대로 살게 되는 거야.
그럴 때 분명하게 말해 보면 어떨까?
“나 술 안 좋아해!”라고 할 수 있지
그 친구가 술을 마셨다면 어떻게 해야 할까?
술을 마신 친구의 차를 타면 어떤 일이 생길지 생각해 봐.
술을 마시고 운전하는 습관이 있는 사람이랑
같이 있게 될 수 있는 상황을 피하는 거야.
문제가 생길 때 타고 갈 다른 교통 수단도 미리 생각해 두고.
술이 꼭 있어야 즐거운 시간을 보낼 수 있는 건 아냐.
그런 생각을 가진 사람들이랑 애써 어울리려고 하지 마.

en.text: Many people equate drinking
with having a good time.
But at Proverbs 23:32,
the Bible says that alcohol
can ‘bite like a snake.’
Are there laws on drinking alcohol where you live?
If so, you could be fined,
be sentenced to community service,
lose your freedom to drive,
or even go to jail.
Even if none of those things happen,
alcohol can lower your inhibitions
—and not in a good way.
Under the influence, you could say or do things
you’ll later regret.
But what if you’re at a party
and unexpectedly find
that some are drinking and heading for trouble?
What would you do?
The Bible says that an intelligent person
sees trouble coming and avoids it.
Stop and think.
What might happen if you stay?
How could you leave before trouble comes
without inviting ridicule?
Here’s a tip:
Make a plan with your parents
to call or text if you need to leave early.
How about this?
What would you do if someone pressures you to drink?
At Romans 6:16, the Bible indicates
that when you let others control your decisions,
you become their slave.
You could just follow along
and let your peers rule your life.
Or you could give a firm response
—perhaps something like,
“No thanks!” or “Sorry, I’m not into that!”
What if you’re out with friends
and realize the driver has been drinking?
According to the Bible,
the person who spends time with fools “will fare badly.”
What could happen if you let that person drive you home?
What other options do you have?
Try this:
Avoid situations where you’ll be with a driver
who has a reputation for drinking and driving.
Always have a Plan B for transportation.
Remember, you don’t have to drink to have a good time,
and you don’t have to associate with people
who think that you do.
Have the courage to think past the drink.

en.text: We welcome all of you to the December program
of JW Broadcasting!
This month we have something different
to share with you.
The Governing Body has decided
that Gilead graduations
and the spiritual portion
of the annual meeting programs
will be featured as monthly JW Broadcasting programs each year.
At this time, you will be able to watch the first part
of the graduation of the 143rd class of Gilead.
You will enjoy listening to the five Scriptural talks
that will each be introduced to you
by Brother Herd of the Governing Body.
Most languages that our monthly program is produced in
did not have the resources to also translate
and produce the Gilead graduation.
Now, by using the graduation as the monthly program,
many more of our brothers and sisters around the world
will be able to enjoy this rich spiritual banquet.
We now invite you to enjoy Part One of the graduation
of the 143rd class of Gilead!
It’s graduation day
for this 143rd class of Gilead.
And it’s been a long time coming
with a lot of work, worry, sweat,
and nerve-racking parts given
in front of your instructors and fellow classmates.
Wow! Ooh.
But none of you received
a failing grade —not one.
You’re going to graduate today.
This is your day.
And it’s a joyful day, isn’t it?
A very joyful day for you,
and a joyful day for each and every one of us.
We’re glad you came to Gilead school,
and it saddens us a bit to know you are leaving us.
You’re not going to be here much longer.
Your fine spiritual instructors
—Brothers Cauthon, Lippold,
Noumair, Samuelson, and Stovall
—they would like to cry, but they’re good manly men,
and it’s hard for good manly men to cry in public.
Of course, there is a host of others
—too many to name—
such as Sam Herd.
Oops, it just slipped out beyond my control.
Your instructors have done a fine job of helping you
to open your eyes to see your “Grand Instructor”
mentioned at Isaiah 30:20.
After all, he is the one who has been teaching
by giving his holy spirit
to all these brothers that I’ve mentioned.
Look at what is stated at Isaiah 66:1
—66:1—it says: “This is what Jehovah says:
‘The heavens are my throne, and the earth is my footstool.’”
For the last five months, you’ve been sitting at Jehovah’s feet
and you have been taught by your Grand Instructor.
What you have learned is much more than you knew
when you first sat down five months ago.
Without a doubt, the knowledge you have taken in
has brought you closer to Jehovah.
You have really drawn close to Jehovah,
and he has drawn close to you.
However, you’ve only scratched the surface.
Job said: . . .
[Indiscernible whispering]
Did you hear what I said?
Of course you didn’t.
Now let’s read the scripture,
“Look! These are just the fringes of his ways;
only a faint whisper has been heard of him!”
This is just about as much as we have learned
compared to what Jehovah knows.
Who knows all that Jehovah knows?
No one —not even Jesus,
and he knows quite a bit more than we do.
He’s been around longer, hasn’t he?
Much longer.
In fact, Jesus was present when the earth was created.
When was that?
Well, if you’ve been listening to morning worship,
you’ll know that one member of the Governing Body
told us that in Proverbs chapter 8
—he says take a look at that—
verses 29 and 30, and he read it to us, he said: “This is what it says.”
“When he established the foundations of the earth,
then I was beside him as a master worker.”
Do you remember that?
You don’t if you didn’t hear today’s text or read it.
But we are convinced that you heard it and you read it.
Well, that’s a long time, isn’t it?
The earth —foundations of the earth—
how long?
Well, based on the very old zircon rock from Australia,
some scientists say we know that the earth
is at least four and one-half billion years old,
give or take a hundred million years.
Well, no one really knows down here on earth,
but we have to listen to some of these so-called wise men.
Jesus, in his prehuman existence, was there.
There’s no doubt about that.
Colossians chapter 1 shows that, that he was there.
He was at Jehovah’s side way before then
—listening and learning.
And he’s at Jehovah’s side today, isn’t he?
You know that.
He’s right there seated beside Jehovah,
doing the work that Jehovah has outlined that should be done.
When measured by Jesus, we’re newborn infants.
We barely have our eyes open, barely.
What we see is not what we’re going to see
in the years to come.
We’re just looking; we’re just learning;
we’re touching things —and for the first time.
Just think, in the past ten years
how many things we’ve touched for the first time.
Even though we’ve read the Bible over and over again,
and we’ve listened to it being read to us over and over again,
but we’ve just touched a few things
—like the generation, 20 years ago, the generation.
And now we know all about that generation, right?
And so many other things —dragnet—
many other things,
like the sanctification of God’s name,
vindication of his sovereignty —touch, touch, touch.
You Gilead students, you’ve touched a few things,
but not everything,
not everything.
But what you have learned,
put to good use in your assignments.
Keep in mind that you don’t know it all.
And here’s something else: You never will.
No matter how long we live, we’ll never know it all.
Jehovah will still be revealing things to us,
and they’re always good things.
We benefit from what Jehovah gives us.
He knows exactly what we need, and he gives it to us.
So always keep that in mind.
We’re students under Jehovah,
and that’s where we’ll always be.
But we’re happy.
We’re glad to be here.
We’re glad to be here with you students,
every one of you, and you’re good students too.
Now it’s true, not all of you are A-plus students.
I’m not either.
I was happy to get a good C-plus in school.
Well, we’re going to get started now with a major part of our meeting.
“Being Happy Despite Challenges”
is the theme of Brother Gerrit Lösch’s talk.
Brother Lösch is a member of the Governing Body.
He is the senior member of the Governing Body.
Now, I mean by that, he’s been a member of the Governing Body
longer than the rest of us.
I’m the oldest one on the Governing Body.
We all face challenges of some sort.
So let’s listen carefully to what he has to say, Brother Lösch.
“Oh happy day.”
These are the first words of the gospel song.
And it goes on to say,
“Oh happy day, when Jesus washed my sins away.”
And we can agree
with these music lyrics
from the 18th century.
We agree that forgiveness of sins makes us happy, doesn’t it?
But for many others,
the happy day is the payday at the end of the month.
Now, what is a happy day for you students?
Graduation day.
But you are not happy because it’s over,
but because you had the privilege to attend Gilead.
Many in the world believe that if they had more money,
they would be happier.
However, many who made gaining of wealth
the chief goal in life now suffer disappointment.
Some have lost their house,
being unable to pay the mortgage when they were laid off from work.
Wealth does not bring happiness.
Rather, lasting happiness comes from doing Jehovah’s will.
What is happiness?
Happiness is a state of well-being,
contentment, even deep and intense joy.
But in the world, many are unhappy.
In 2015, there were more than twice as many suicides
in the United States
—namely 44,193—
more than homicides,
where there were only 17,000 of those.
Up to 120 people take their life
in the United States each day.
How sad.
Though very rare, due to depression
even some true Christians have taken their life,
but generally we are a happy people, aren’t we?
And here are 12 reasons for our happiness.
For one, we can be happy because we worship a happy God.
Psalm 33:12:
“Happy is the nation whose God is Jehovah.”
Secondly, because we have our sins forgiven,
as mentioned in the introduction.
Romans 4:7 says:
“Happy are those whose lawless deeds
have been pardoned and whose sins have been covered.”
Number three, we can be happy
because we’re being loved by Jehovah and Jesus.
Four, we’re happy because of being united
with our worldwide brotherhood.
Five, we can be happy because of living in a spiritual paradise,
having peace with Jehovah, with our brothers,
and also having plenty of spiritual food.
Six, in the Sermon on the Mount,
Jesus emphasized spirituality when he said:
“Happy are those conscious of their spiritual need.”
In this sermon, he mentioned nine things that make us happy.
What things?
Well, you’ll find out by rereading this sermon.
Number seven, we are happy because our life has meaning,
namely, according to Ephesians 1:12,
to “serve for the praise of his glory.”
Number eight, at Revelation 1:3,
Jesus showed that reading God’s Word makes us happy.
He says: “Happy is [he] who reads aloud
and those who hear the words of this prophecy.”
Do you want to be happy every day?
Read the Bible every day.
In the book of Revelation, Jesus proclaims seven happinesses.
Which ones?
Find out by rereading Revelation.
Number nine, we are also happy
because we serve in the spiritual temple.
In Revelation 7, not just the anointed
but also the great crowd are shown serving,
not near or before, but in the temple.
David called the Levites happy.
He said at Psalm 65:4:
“Happy is the one whom you choose
[to] bring near to reside in your courtyards.”
David arranged the Levites
so that they could serve at the temple twice a year for one week.
However, in contrast, all of God’s people serve him
in the spiritual temple all year long, every day.
How happy we can be.
Number ten, Psalm 40:4 says:
“Happy is the man who trusts in Jehovah.”
Trust is a must to maintain happiness.
When you arrive in your assignment,
trust that Jehovah will support you.
Trust in Jehovah’s strength
rather than in your Gilead training and your abilities.
If low on funds, trust in Jehovah.
He will care for you.
If you have to learn a new language, trust.
When you are being accused wrongly,
trust that matters will be clarified in time.
When you are discouraged, trust in better times.
There is light at the end of each tunnel.
Number 11, we are happy because we practice giving,
and Jesus said:
“There is more happiness in giving than there is in receiving.”
Words well-known —Acts 20:35.
And 12, we are happy because of the wonderful promise
of a heavenly paradise for some
and an earthly paradise for billions.
We are happy because this is tied to the promise of everlasting life.
How does happiness show?
It shows by a spirit of appreciation and expressions of appreciation.
So beware of a complaining spirit.
When Jehovah liberated Israel, the people were happy.
However, within just a few weeks,
they complained and even wanted to return to slavery in Egypt.
To stay happy, have a positive outlook.
Don’t complain about the thorns on rosebushes,
but be glad that some thornbushes have roses on it.
Number two, when you go to your assignment,
radiate the happiness you feel.
Let others see it in your eyes,
in your face, in your smile;
but smile, not like a salesperson, but smile from the heart.
Happiness is also shown by enjoying singing.
Happy people often sing.
Do we sing from time to time?
singing in the rain?
or maybe in the shower? or wherever?
How can we deepen our happiness?
What others do affects our happiness,
and what we do affects the happiness of others.
We simply cannot escape the fact that our happiness
is intertwined with the lives of many other people
—our families, our friends, and others.
Happiness is often in small things,
and unhappiness is the result of neglecting small things.
Happiness is not the absence of challenges,
but the ability to overcome them.
Happiness does not depend on outside circumstances,
but on your inner thoughts
and your relationship with our happy God.
Happiness is connected with joy,
and joy is part of the fruitage of the spirit.
So avail yourself of the holy spirit,
and you will be happier.
You can be happy though hungry.
That was the title of a special talk.
Of course, you can be happy if you’re not hungry.
Perhaps you take advantage of the “happy hour”
in a restaurant where prices are reduced.
You can be happy though single.
You can be happy because of being married
and sometimes despite being married.
You can be happy without children,
and you can be happy despite children.
You can be happy though you’re only 15 years old,
and you can be happy although you’re 85 years of age.
You can be happy though you are sick
and even more happy, of course, if you’re healthy.
You can even be happy though you lost loved ones in death.
You will see them again.
You can be happy though persecuted for Christ’s sake.
Jesus said at Luke 6:22, 23:
“Happy are you whenever men hate you . . .
Rejoice in that day and leap for joy.”
You can be happy if you lost your job.
You can be happy if you lost your wallet.
You can be happy if you lost your heart
in San Francisco
—according to one song— or somewhere else.
You cannot be happy if you lost your mind,
or maybe you can be even happier then
because of not being aware of all the problems
around you and affecting you.
If you are happy, you make others happy.
If you are unhappy, you make others unhappy.
If you are not happy with others,
others will not be happy with you.
Humor adds to happiness.
It makes pain and problems more bearable.
Find happiness in small things
—the sunset, the clouds in the sky, the birds chirping,
the butterfly on the flower, the dog chasing its tail.
Maintain happiness by meditating on the Paradise to come.
Keep it in expectation.
Daniel 12:12 says:
“Happy is the one who keeps in expectation.”
In Paradise, there will be no more tears,
no emotional pain, no unhappiness.
Everyone will be happy every day, all the time.
So let us maintain and deepen our happiness despite challenges
by praising our happy God, Jehovah,
and making others and ourselves ever more happy.
We certainly want to thank you, Brother Lösch.
You made all of us happy with that wonderful talk.
Our next speaker is Brother Gary Breaux,

notice Jehovah’s ability to forget here,

is the work that we do and the various assignments

I’d like to tell you about a brother that really understands

Well, let’s go back to Hebrews 6:10

Jehovah looks down: ‘Thank you very much.

that are important to understand.

you’ve heard all kinds of examples about showing love;
you have every reason to show love.

Practice what you have learned.
Remember if it’s only words, what did Paul say?
It’s like a cymbal —clashing cymbal.
So love means action;
it doesn’t just mean words.
I’d like to tell you another little story
about a brother that had somewhat of a difficulty with this.

At one circuit assembly, his wife wasn’t there,
so he didn’t tell anybody why she wasn’t there,

Then they introduced him. He didn’t come out.

“Who am I, O Jehovah God?”
Do you know who asked that question?
I don’t.
So let’s give our attention to Brother Patrick LaFranca,
a helper to the Personnel Committee of the Governing Body
and a member of the Branch Committee.
He will give us the answer.
Gilead students,
have you ever asked yourself,
‘Who am I to have been invited to Gilead school?’
That’s a good question, isn’t it?
Because very few of God’s people,
relatively speaking, have had that privilege.
So why you?
Was it because you were smarter or better looking
than the average servant of Jehovah?
No, it was because of your spiritual qualities.
And foremost among those was humility.
You have been humble.
But maintaining humility
is a definite spiritual challenge
—not just for you but for all of us, really.
We’ve all inherited the tendency to exalt ourselves.
You think of Adam and Eve.
In the act of profound arrogance,
they wanted to put themselves in God’s place.
They seemed to forget who they were
—creatures made of dust.
So we all have to fight against prideful tendencies.
Humility is elusive.
As soon as we think we are humble, we’ve lost it.
However, Jehovah gives us help.
In the Bible, there are many examples of those who did maintain humility,
and one of these is David.
Let’s just follow David’s life a bit
—different stages of his life— and see, did he maintain humility?
Well, was he humble as a young man?
You remember how Jehovah directed the prophet Samuel
to go to Jesse’s house and annoint one of Jesse’s sons
as the future king of Israel.
Well, seven of his sons were there,
but not one of them was chosen.
And finally, Samuel said, ‘Are these all your sons?’
‘No, there’s David out in the fields shepherding the sheep.’
So they called David,
and Samuel anoints this young man
to be the future king of Israel.
David must have been surprised at this singular privilege that he had.
Now, did he become high-minded?
How would he have treated his brothers
—his older brothers— had he become prideful?
Well, he could have said to Eliab:
‘Well, I guess you got taken down a peg or two, didn’t you?
‘You better start respecting me.
‘And Abinadab,
‘isn’t it time for you to go out now and shepherd the sheep?
‘I have a more important assignment.
‘I have to learn to be king.
Hmm, how can I get into the king’s court?’
No, nothing indicates that David felt that way about himself.
He was content to wait on Jehovah for future privileges.
Is there a lesson here for us?
Yes, you may get future privileges,
but you may have to wait for them.
Go back to your pastures; shepherd the sheep.
So after some time, David is still in the pastures,
and what happens?
An attendant of King Saul
recommends that David serve in the king’s court.
Listen to this recommendation
at 1 Samuel 16:18:
“One of the attendants said:
“‘Look! I have seen how a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite
“‘plays skillfully,
“‘and he is a courageous, mighty warrior.
“‘He can speak well, and he is handsome,
and Jehovah is with him.’”
My, what an impressive recommendation!
So, humble David goes from the sheepfold
to the king’s court as a court musician.
But more privileges followed.
You’ll see in verse 21b that he became Saul’s armor bearer.
And later, David had many exploits in war.
He became famous.
Women sang about his victories.
So fame, good looks,
youth, eloquence,
musical skills, military prowess, divine favor
—David had it all, didn’t he?
And any one of those things could have made him arrogant and prideful,
but it seems that they did not.
Note David’s reaction when King Saul
offered David his daughter in marriage.
That is at 1 Samuel 18:18:
“At this David said to Saul:
“‘Who am I and who are my relatives,
“‘my father’s family in Israel,
for me to become son-in-law to the king?’”
Yes, being related to the king
might have given David reason to boast,
but his words “who am I” resonate with us.
David felt unworthy of being related to the king.
Is there any lesson, perhaps, in this for us?
Well, we may work with and come into contact
with prominent brothers in God’s organization.
In conversations with others, do we drop their names,
trying to make ourselves, perhaps, seem more important?
But now we come to another period in David’s life.
He is now the king of Israel with his capital in Jerusalem,
and he’s dwelling in a royal palace.
And he’s being— He’s feeling very embarrassed
because here he is in a royal palace and the ark of Jehovah,
who is the real king of Israel, is in a tent.
And so he says to the prophet Nathan,
‘I want to build Jehovah a worthy house —a temple.’
But Jehovah says, ‘No, not you,
but one of your sons will do that.’
However, then Jehovah did something
that took David completely by surprise.
God tells him, ‘Instead of you building me a house,
I am going to build a house for you.’
And he makes a covenant with David
so that the kingship would remain
in the family line of David forever.
Well, how did David react?
Please open to 1 Chronicles 17:16-18:
“At that King David came in and sat down before Jehovah and said:
“‘Who am I, O Jehovah God?
“‘And what is my house that you have brought me this far?
“‘As if this were not enough, O God,
“‘you also speak about the house of your servant
“‘down to a distant future time,
“‘and you have looked on me as if I were a man
“‘who should be further exalted, O Jehovah God.
“‘What more can your servant David say to you
“‘about the honor given me
when you know your servant so well?’”
So this marvelous promise
that Jehovah made to David touches his heart,
and he sits before Jehovah in humility,
feeling so unworthy and insignificant.
And later, David made an enormous contribution
for the building of the temple
that by today’s standards
would amount to over 1,200,000,000 dollars.
But in prayer to Jehovah, he says,
as recorded at 1 Chronicles 29:14:
“And yet, who am I . . .
“For everything is from you,
and what we have given to you comes from your own hand.”
What a humble spirit.
And it’s true, isn’t it?
Whatever we give to Jehovah,
it’s something that he has already given to us.
It’s no wonder that Jehovah God loved David.
He was a man really agreeable to God’s own heart.
How can we cultivate and maintain such a humble heart?
It’s not simply by saying,
“I am determined to be humble.”
No, but do as David did.
Once in a while, sit down, take a long look at your life,
and see what blessings, what undeserved kindnesses,
Jehovah has extended to you.
Ponder over his awesomeness.
And when we do so, we will be moved to say to Jehovah:
‘Who am I, Jehovah God, that you’ve honored me,
‘making me one of your fellow workers despite my many flaws?
‘Who am I, Jehovah,
‘that you’ve given me health and strength
‘to serve in my assignment?
‘Who am I, O God, to have this special privilege of service
when I know there are many more and more deserving than I?’
Of course, there is a wholesome pride
in having the privilege of being one of God’s servants,
but it is an unhealthy pride
that makes one feel superior.
And if we are looking down on others,
we cannot be looking up at Jehovah.
And that really is the secret of maintaining humility
—to know what we really are.
We always keep Jehovah before us as David did.
So students, we have every confidence
that you will keep your eyes on your awesome God,
and that he will use you and he will bless you
even more than he has on this day of your graduation.
Well, I don’t know about you, but I was enlightened
by “Who Am I, O Jehovah God?”
That was David that said that.
Well, live and learn.
Brother James Cauthon,
one of our Theocratic Schools instructors,
will speak on the theme “Sympathetic Strings.”
Imagine that you had the means
to give everyone in your life
an expensive gift.
You know what would happen?
They would be happy.
You would be happier because you would experience
what Jesus said is a greater happiness —giving.
Actually, you can give others
something that is very special
—something they really need— and it won’t cost you a cent.
What is it?
It’s your attention.
Romans 12:15,
the apostle Paul wrote this, he said:
“Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.”
We need to learn to understand and share another person’s feelings
whether it’s joy or sadness.
But why?
We need to understand it
because we’re living in “critical times hard to deal with.”
And so when the Bible says to “weep with those who weep,”
we can sum that up in two words:
Show sympathy.
Why should we do that?
Well, going back to Romans 12, and this time in verse 5,
notice what we’re reminded of.
Paul wrote: “So we, although many, are one body in union with Christ,
but individually we are members belonging to one another.”
Now this, of course, was written with those of the new covenant in mind,
but in reality all of us as Jehovah’s people
belong to one another.
Now, you might find it interesting to know that in the Christian Greek Scriptures,
there are some 50 “one another” commands:
Love one another, encourage one another,
incite one another, pray for one another, and other things.
The Watchtower said this, it said:
“We should be sensitive to the pains and heartaches of our brothers and sisters.
“Often, we can bring much relief to fellow believers
“who are suffering emotional pain
“if we take the time to listen to them
with a truly sympathetic ear.”
Sympathy is entering in
and sharing in the pain of others.
Now, sometimes in English we say “empathy.”
It’s also translated “fellow feeling” or even “feel pity.”
But it’s in times of crisis, grief, and doubt
when we need one another the most.
So how can we show that we care?
The answer is simple: Listen sympathetically.
The effect can be likened to the sympathetic strings that are used
to enhance the sound and harmony of certain musical instruments.
Now, all of these have strings that are not played,
but they react to the strings that are struck
or plucked, if you would,
thus they become sympathetic.
They produce a unique harmony.
It’s a oneness, really.
The effect of this
is something that is very special.
But now, how this actually works can be demonstrated with the use
of two tuning forks.
Notice the one reacts to being struck.
The second, although not being struck,
reacts to the feelings of the first.
So the first fork is no longer alone.
It has become joined by a second fork
that is now also picking up the vibrations
and is said to be sympathetic.
It’s a harmony, really.
After the loss of a loved one, one sister said:
“Tears became the language of my heart.
I so appreciated it when the friends came over and just cried with me.”
Sure, it’s a oneness —a harmony.
She felt it.
We recognize, though, that there is a certain caution here
because sharing joy is one thing,
but sympathetically listening to another’s pain of heart
can be emotionally taxing
and time-consuming.
As our illustration demonstrates,
even after the original fork is removed,
the sympathetic one is still feeling the effects,
isn’t that right?
And that’s why, whether we like it or not,
our actions will reveal what’s really in our hearts
when it comes to our brothers and sisters.
Going back to Romans again,
this time Romans 12:10,
we’re reminded of this.
It says: “In brotherly love have tender affection for one another.”
Listening is a simple gesture of affection.
Often the problem, of course, is that we’re in such a hurry to fix things
that we feel that we can’t take the time
to listen to someone else or to sympathize with them.
Or sometimes we’re so preoccupied with our own hurts
that we’re caught up in that.
But self-pity will smother sympathy for others.
And we need to be careful, frankly,
because sometimes we feel
that we just have to solve the problem right away,
so we make statements
that are not helpful to the person that is suffering.
‘You know, you need to just toughen up.’
Or here’s one of my favorites:
‘Others suffered, now it’s your turn.’
Or comparisons: ‘Well, at least you can walk.’
Well, we don’t mean those things to be malicious,
but how do they come across?
You see, they come across as condescending.
And it’s another way of saying,
“I don’t care” or “I don’t care enough.”
Job tried ten times
to explain to his comforters his feelings.
And finally, after the tenth time, he said,
‘Oh, if someone would but listen to me.’
His hurt, his pain, was enhanced
because of his companions’ failure to listen.
How sad that is.
They neither cared about Job,
nor did they want to understand his feelings.
They shut him down.
Could we ever do
the same thing or something similar?
How sad that would be.
To share in someone’s grief and pain, you must be willing to listen,
you must be willing to take the time,
and you must care more about them than you do yourself.
We need to learn to take ourself out of the equation.
Romans 12:10 continues:
“In showing honor to one another, take the lead.”
We honor others by being nonjudgmental,
by taking them seriously,
and by giving sincere heartfelt attention and consideration
to their words and their feelings.
We need to remember this point:
That is, that our relationship with God
and our relationship with our brothers is one and the same.
Let me repeat that.
Our relationship with God
and our relationship with our brothers is one and the same.
Jehovah cares deeply about how we interact with one another.
Jehovah wants his people to be known
for their love for one another more than anything else.
So your gift
of sympathetic concern
will be a powerful means of showing love
and restoring a measure of harmony into the lives of others.
With talks like that, I can see why I’m not one of the instructors.
The illustration of the two forks just drove the point home, didn’t it?
Well, here’s another,
“The Glowing Coal” is the theme Brother Mark Noumair has chosen.
He’s also one of the Theocratic Schools instructors
and a helper to the Teaching Committee of the Governing Body.
Brother Noumair, we are burning with anticipation.
On joyous occasions as today,
your love burns strong, and rightly so.
Remember this day.
Etch indelibly in your minds how you feel right now
because this love that is burning brightly within you
will be tested.
When we undergo trials,
reviewing Bible accounts of faithful men and women
can bolster our own faith.
And we can hear their words ringing in our minds.
But what about those who have never spoken a word
recorded in the Bible?
Can their silent examples of faith help us?
Let’s consider one.
Her name is Rizpah.
We know very little about her.
She is first introduced to us as a concubine of King Saul.
No doubt, she must have been very beautiful to catch the attention of the king.
However, her life was not an easy one.
In time,
Saul —the father of her children—
is killed in battle.
She now becomes the property of Saul’s son, Ishbosheth.
He too is killed.
Unfortunately, Rizpah’s most painful test
was yet to come.
Long after Saul’s death, Jehovah tells King David
that bloodguilt remains on Saul’s house
because of his attempt to annihilate the Gibeonites,
which violated an ancient covenant.
Thus, the entire nation of Israel is guilty
of shedding innocent blood.
How does David resolve this issue?
Second Samuel 21:3
shows what David did.
Second Samuel 21:3, David asks the Gibeonites:
“What should I do for you?”
Verse 6, they answer:
“Let seven of [Saul’s] sons be given to us.
We will hang their dead bodies before Jehovah.”
Verse 6 continues, David said:
“I will hand them over.”
Who does David hand over?
He hands over, in verse 8, Rizpah’s two sons,
“the two sons of Rizpah,”
the two people in the whole world that she loved most.
What a heartbreaking tragedy for Rizpah,
but she could do nothing about it.
The decision was made; it was out of her control.
Eventually, all seven men are hung.
Now, under the Mosaic Law, those executed upon a stake
should have been taken down before nightfall and buried.
Burial would have brought closure to this mother’s crushed soul.
And above all, it would conform
to Jehovah’s requirements for the dignity of life
and that proper disposal of the dead body
would have been according to Jehovah’s instructions.
Undoubtedly, Rizpah knows this,
but it didn’t happen that way.
So can you feel her anguish as night approaches
and no one comes to take those bodies down?
And Rizpah could have been thinking:
‘But the Mosaic Law, no one is following the Law.
It’s not right.’
But there was a catch.
It seems that the Gibeonites
were allowed to follow a different procedure in this instance
because a national sin had been committed by King Saul.
Now did Rizpah know that?
We don’t know.
But what we do know, one day goes by;
the Law is not followed.
The bodies are not taken down.
Two days go by; three days go by.
What does she do?
Well, according to verse 10,
Rizpah continues day after day
in the blaze of that scorching summer sun.
In fact, verse 10 says what she did do.
It says that “she did not allow the birds of the heavens
“to land on [those bodies] by day
nor the wild beasts of the field to come near by night.”
There she was out there, day after day, shooing those birds away
—not to draw attention to herself, not to get justice for her sons, no.
She understood, she appreciated,
and she upheld Jehovah’s view of human life.
She allowed Jehovah’s values to shape her behavior
even at great personal cost.
You must love this woman.
Although Rizpah probably didn’t understand exactly why things were happening this way
—why was it turning out in this way—
this different procedure of not burying her sons
had a major impact on her personal life.
Yet, her conduct showed her love for Jehovah
and the loyalty that she had for his arrangements
—that this love and loyalty burned brightly within her.
Here’s your big lesson.
Now, at times, you might feel that your life is outside of your control.
You may go through a trial
that allows Jehovah’s standards and decisions to shape you,
perhaps at great personal cost.
For example, you’re familiar with theocratic procedure;
you’re familiar with theocratic policies.
We know that.
But there might come a time when an organizational direction
—an organizational procedure—
is modified for reasons that you are not fully aware of,
and that decision affects you personally.
What will you do?
Like Rizpah, keep doing what you can under your circumstances.
Shoo those birds away —those negative thoughts.
Stir up that fire.
Don’t allow your warmth and glow for Jehovah God to burn out.
Now, days go by,
according to verse 9 and verse 10:
‘from the start of the harvest to the rain.’
Now this implies that this may have been five to six months
that she kept vigil over her sons’ bodies.
What could she have been thinking about during this time
that may have been close to half a year?
What would she have been thinking about?
‘How could David be so uncaring as not to command
‘to give my boys a proper burial.
‘And Jehovah,
‘after all that I’ve been through,
where are you, Jehovah?’
Now these might have been natural thoughts, true.
Yet, if she did have them,
she did not allow these thoughts to put out the fire
of her love for God or to make her bitter.
Perhaps others even tried to discourage her saying:
‘Go home. Give up.’
But she didn’t.
Nor did she start a campaign by gathering others to her side.
There’s no record of her bad-mouthing David,
criticizing his decision as unfair.
Nor did she presume to take the bodies down herself.
‘Well, if nobody is going to do it, I’ll do it.’
No, in spite of all of these difficulties
—imagine— that Rizpah was suffering,
she still had embers of love
for Jehovah God glowing brightly
that moved her to stay loyal,
remain in her place,
and wait on David to make the decision.
Did her faithful endurance really matter?
Did anyone notice her plight?
Verse 11:
“David was told
what Saul’s concubine Rizpah . . . had done.”
So imagine someone goes to David:
‘David, there’s this Rizpah; she’s up there near these bodies.
She’s shooing these birds away.’
So, what did David do?
Did he now, finally, give Rizpah’s sons a decent burial?
Actually, he did more.
Verses 12 through 14
show how David had the bones of Saul
and the bones of Jonathan brought all the way from Jabesh-gilead
—which might have taken a journey of about 100 miles (160 km)—
and buried those bones with the bones of Rizpah’s sons
in Saul’s family plot in Benjamite territory.
So in the end, Rizpah got more than she expected.
She saw the bones of her sons
and their father buried together.
Rizpah didn’t see that coming,
but it was worth the wait.
So, what’s the big lesson we want you to remember here?
Rizpah’s love and loyalty and endurance
provides an example worth imitating.
When you go through a trial,
remember that others are observing your conduct
—they’re watching.
And out of frustration, you might feel:
‘Well, why haven’t, why haven’t the elders done anything?
‘Why aren’t the overseers taking care of this situation?
Jehovah, why don’t you do something?’
And Jehovah is saying: ‘I am doing something.
‘I’m using your silent example
‘to show others that when you endure a situation,
‘I will reward them.
‘I’ll reward them more than they ever anticipated,
‘and it will be worth the wait.
Because I, Jehovah, I love being a rewarder.’
What a noble and honorable way to be used by Jehovah God.
Now, Rizpah was not a victim of her circumstances.
Rather, she became a victor over her adversities.
The intense heat of her trials did not break her as a person
nor crush her desire to please Jehovah God.
So little is known about her,
and yet we learn so much from her.
She never had one spoken word recorded in the Bible,
yet Jehovah must have been very impressed with this remarkable woman.
Her name and example earned a place in his sacred Book
and is worthy of our examination.
She teaches you
—she teaches you how to take life’s indignities with dignity.
So, what helped her endure successfully?
Perhaps a clue is in her name.
It literally means “Glowing Coal.”
Now, we don’t know why she was given that name, true.
But like a piece of coal glowing warm and bright,
Rizpah kept her thoughts focused on love for her sons’ loyalty to Jehovah,
loyalty to his arrangements,
confident that relief would eventually come.
She was industrious.
She actively guarded her sons’ bodies from being eaten by animals.
She didn’t allow negative feelings to shut her down and extinguish her love.
Rather, in the face of what she might have felt to be an injustice,
she did what she could.
So, what do we want you to remember?
What do we want you to go away with to your assignments thinking about?
In the face of a perceived injustice, keep working;
keep carrying out your assigned work assignments;
keep doing what you can.
Shoo away those birds.
Stoke up the fire of your love for Jehovah God and the brothers.
And wait on Jehovah to resolve any pending issues,
confident that relief will come now or in the new world.
It will be worth that wait.
And yet, above all, above all, be a Rizpah.
Under all circumstances,
keep your love for God burning brightly like a glowing coal.
Those talks were inspiring to the students of the 143rd class,
and I am sure that you feel much the same way after viewing them.
But you probably are wondering, ‘What about the rest of the program?’
Wonder no longer.
Part 2 and Part 3 will be posted on the Video on Demand section
of JW Broadcasting later this month.
In fact, Part 2 is a video entitled The Inside Story.
It is scheduled to be posted next Monday, December 11.
You will enjoy hearing experiences from some of the graduates of the class.
Until the next monthly program, this is JW Broadcasting
coming to you from the world headquarters of Jehovah’s Witnesses.

en.text: An introduction to the book of Zechariah.
Zechariah began to prophesy
in Jerusalem in 520 B.C.E.,
17 years after the return
from Babylonian exile.
He prophesied for at least two years,
completing the book bearing his name
in 518 B.C.E.
His work overlapped
that of the prophet Haggai.
The rebuilding of Jehovah’s temple was at a standstill.
It appeared to observers that Jehovah had forsaken the city.
The people there were discouraged
and focused on personal comforts.
Jehovah sent Zechariah to join the prophet Haggai
in encouraging the Jews to resume the temple construction
despite all obstacles.
Did you know?
Solomon’s temple was completed
in just over seven years.
In contrast,
when Zechariah wrote his book,
the reconstruction had been under way
for about 20 years
but without completion.
The book of Zechariah contains 14 chapters.
Chapters 1 to 6
set forth a series of intriguing visions
that ensured divine backing of the work of rebuilding the temple
and the return to pure worship.
For example,
one vision features a woman named Wickedness
who is put into a container
and taken far away by two winged women.
This illustrates that wickedness has no place
among Jehovah’s people.
Chapters 7 and 8 urge God’s people
to turn from unjust treatment of the poor
and to deal with one another in loyal love and mercy.
Chapter 10 foretells
Jehovah’s turning his favorable attention to his repentant people.
Zechariah also recorded
several significant prophecies about the Christ.
He indicated that the future King of God’s Kingdom
would triumphantly enter Jerusalem on a donkey.
Zechariah foretold God’s true Shepherd
would be betrayed for 30 pieces of silver.
Zechariah also foretold details
about this Messianic Shepherd’s death.
Chapter 14 states
that Jehovah forms a very great valley.
This valley is for the protection of his people
and results in a complete triumph of true worship.
As you study the book of Zechariah,
notice how Jehovah makes his work succeed despite adversity,
how he describes the future King of his Kingdom,
and how his loyal subjects will remain safe in his valley of protection.

It all started first thing this morning.
Everyone was signing a birthday card for one of our classmates, Lucas.
Do you want to sign the birthday card for Lucas?
He just got home from being at the hospital for cancer treatments.
No thanks.
I’m a Jehovah’s Witness, and I don’t celebrate birthdays.
What?
Hum?
That’s rude.
Come on, sign it!
You guys, you guys, Aiden—
My teacher said that Lucas may not come back to school for a long time.
I felt so bad he was sick.
Aiden, Aiden, can you think about it?
The thing is, I did want to sign the card.
Lucas was one of the nicest people in my class.
Maybe I can just sign it.
I mean, it’s not like I’m going to a birthday party.
Hey, little man. How are you doing?
Yeah?
Mom said you had a rough day today.
When Dad came in, I told him everything that happened.
I know from the Bible that it’s wrong to celebrate birthdays.
But is signing the card really a big deal?
Dad said my question was a good one.
Then he showed me a scripture.
Do you want to get your Bible for me?
Let’s look in Ephesians 5.
Ephesians 5:10:
“Keep on making sure of what is acceptable to the Lord.”
He said, “We all have to keep making sure
“of what’s acceptable to Jehovah
because Satan is a master at tricking us.”
Then he used the example of Aaron.
The Israelites asked Aaron to make them a god.
So Aaron made a golden calf,
thinking that it could represent Jehovah.
He told the people:
“There is a festival to Jehovah tomorrow.”
But true worship was being mixed with false worship,
and Jehovah was not happy.
And many were punished.
That example helped me a lot.
I know birthdays are wrong because the Bible teaches
that they are not approved by Jehovah.
But we don’t want to be confused like Aaron
and try to mix true and false worship.
All right, let’s go talk to Mom.
We want to make Jehovah happy.
So Dad said, “It’s always good to ask,
How would Jehovah feel if I did this?”
I still didn’t sign the card, but I’m going to do something else for Lucas.
Can I go see Lucas?
Yeah. Go ahead, Buddy.
He’s right over there.
How have you been feeling?
A little better.
And then I realized something:
Instead of celebrating one day,
I could share with Lucas our hope
of living forever on a beautiful paradise earth.
So there will be no sickness ever again.
They will build houses and have food.
