title: 제141기 길르앗 졸업식: 3부—결론 연설 및 임명

en.text: We’ve come to our principal talk
for this 141st class of Gilead,
the graduation.
And we’re going to invite Brother Gerrit Lösch now.
I thought you’d find this interesting.
This is the 141st class.
We’ve heard that throughout the morning.
Well, 100 classes ago,
Brother Lösch was graduating from the 41st class.
And I don’t know if heaven did it,
but we had an Austrian in each one of those.
So that’s very nice.
And I don’t want to say anything, but he is getting a little older,
but he still looks great, doesn’t he?
Because he knew the sister in this class
when she was just a tiny little girl.
So very nice.
And Brother Lösch gave me that information; so it’s bona fide.
So Brother Lösch is going to speak
on the theme “Make Good Use of Your Time.”
What’s the time? Well, anyway, it’s time to start.
There are certain things of which the richest
and the poorest person on earth have the same:
number one, life; second, two parents;
third, free will;
and fourth, time.
Poor and rich all have 24 hours a day.
Therefore, it’s not quite correct to say
one has “no time” or “plenty of time.”
All have the same—24 hours.
The word “time” is an integral part of our vocabulary.
What is time?
Some say, “Time is money.”
If we make decisions, “time will tell” whether they are good ones.
In the world, some make wrong decisions and then,
therefore, they have to “do time” in prison.
When driving a car, we may “make good time,”
although from “time to time,” we may stop and have a snack.
We are “taking our time” if we do not hurry.
We may still arrive “on time” or even “ahead of time”
if we “time it right.”
But “at times,” we may still be late,
especially if our “timing” was poor,
which may not be “all the time,” just “from time to time.”
After we arrive at our destination,
the “time has arrived” to have a “good time.”
But on a more serious note,
how does the Bible use the term “time”?
Ecclesiastes 3:1 says:
‘There is an appointed time for everything,
‘a time for every activity under the heavens:
‘for birth and for death;
‘to plant, to uproot;
‘to tear down, to build up;
‘to weep and to laugh;
‘to wail and to dance;
a time to keep and a time to throw away,’
like when we have to move to another complex.
It is now the “acceptable time” to preach
because “the appointed times of the nations”
are over and we are living in “the time of the end.”
Therefore, we should be zealous
in line with the urgency of times.
Jehovah blesses the work and said that he
“will speed it up in its own time.”
The Greek adjective ai·oʹni·os can,
as is evident from the context,
signify both “long lasting” and “everlasting.”
From the first man, Adam,
forward, time has been measured in terms of years.
Thus, Adam was 130 years old
when he became father to Seth.
Monthly divisions also came into use.
By the time of the Flood, we find time divided
into months of 30 days,
and a period of five months
is shown in the Bible to equal 150 days.
The same record
also indicates that Noah divided the year into 12 months.
To track time, a calendar is used for dividing time
into years, months, weeks, and days.
The world’s oldest calendar
was discovered in a Scottish field
at Warren Field,
according to BBC News from the year 2013
and National Geographic of July 15, 2013.
It was excavated first in the year 2004 only.
To track time during the day, also, sundials were invented.
They are considered the first
time-measuring devices known to man.
Dating to the 19th dynasty,
or the 13th century before our Common Era,
a few years ago, a sundial was found
on the floor of a workman’s hut
in the Valley of Kings,
the burial place of rulers from Egypt.
In 1675, King Charles II of England
commissioned that a small observatory
be constructed in what is now
the London borough of Greenwich
in order to find out the longitude of places
for perfecting navigation and astronomy.
Two newly invented timepieces
with pendulums 13 feet, or 4 meters, long
were installed to make accurate calculations
of the earth’s rotation.
Noon Greenwich Mean Time is the moment
when the sun reaches its zenith over any point
on the Greenwich longitude line, or meridian,
from Latin meridianus, of midday.
Based on this Latin word, time before noon
came to be known as ante meridiem,
or before midday;
and time after noon
came to be known as post meridiem,
or p.m., as we call it.
Today, time is measured for accuracy with atomic clocks.
They are regulated by atomic vibrations
and are accurate to one second in 80 million years
—very accurate.
Again, what is time?
You have heard the saying
“as time goes by”
or “time flies,”
but this is Scripturally not quite correct.
Time does not go or walk or fly
—we fly.
And this is supported at Psalm 90:10,
where Moses wrote this psalm, not David.
And it says in verse 10:
“The span of our life is 70 years,
“or 80 if one is especially strong.
“But they are filled with trouble and sorrow;
“they quickly pass by,
and away we fly”
—not the time.
When a man dies,
time is still there and hasn’t flown anywhere.
Again, what is time?
Twelve o’clock noon in New York
is twelve o’clock midnight in Mongolia.
When you cross the date line westbound,
suddenly you have lost a day, seemingly.
But did you really lose a day? No.
It’s just the perception.
To the contrary,
when you come from Japan to the United States,
you seem to gain a day
crossing the date line eastbound.
But does this change the reality of time? No.
You have not become a day younger. Sorry.
What’s the time on North Pole, exactly on North Pole?
If you stay on the North Pole, does time move on?
Something to think about.
Really, time is an abstract concept that humans have invented
to explain, compare, and measure what we observe.
Sometimes, time seems to move faster than at other times.
There’s an old saying that “a watched kettle never boils.”
It’s true that when
we are watching time, when we are conscious of it,
when we are waiting for something to happen,
then it seems to pass ever so slowly.
However, if we are busy,
if we are interested in and preoccupied with what we are doing,
then it really appears that time flies.
Moreover, with older people, time seems to pass
much more quickly than with young children.
And why is this?
One year added to the life of a one-year-old
means a 100-percent increase.
One year added to the life of a 50-year-old
means just 2 percent more.
The perception of time is also subject to circumstances.
When a couple in love meets,
they wish time would stand still, is it not so?
But they cannot slow down what is perceived as time.
On the other hand, when somebody is sick in a hospital bed,
he might wish that time would pass more quickly
so he could recover sooner and go home sooner.
But he cannot speed up the passing of time.
Time is an observed phenomenon by means of which
we humans sense and record
changes in our environment and in the universe.
In the universe, time is measured
based on the speed of light, which is a constant.
The Michelson-Morley experiment, around the end of the 19th century,
discovered that the speed of light is the same
regardless of the direction it’s heading
and regardless of the motion
of the originating source.
Light moves at about
300,000 kilometers per second.
It takes about 100,000 years for a beam of light
to travel from just one end of our Milky Way to the other end.
And our Milky Way
is said to have 200 billion stars like the sun.
What you see
when you look up at night to the night sky,
it’s not what is there now,
but what was there in the past.
When a light beam from a star that is a million light years away
hits the earth,
it means that the object that you now see
was there a million years ago.
To see what is there now
and whether the star even still exists,
you need to wait another million years
until the light beam from that place arrives at the earth.
Just imagine!
Looking at the universe, we always look only into the past.
It is estimated that the visible universe
exists for 13 billion years.
Most scientists agree that it had a beginning,
so-called big bang.
The Bible says:
“In the beginning God created,” and that includes the visible universe.
The universe expands in all directions.
Scientists have not found an end of the visible universe
with optical telescopes or radio telescopes.
But if one would continue to travel through space long enough,
logically one should come to an area where there are no more
stars or galaxies, just empty space.
Some known galaxies are moving into that empty space,
or toward that empty space, with about the speed of light.
It’s very impressive.
Some scientists say, “Time does not exist.”
It exists, however, definitely in our perception.
Man invented the concept of time
to be able to measure changes.
Did time always exist?
Well, in Jude 25,
we can read what it says there
from our own Bible.
It says:
“To the only God our Savior through Jesus Christ our Lord,
“be glory, majesty, might, and authority
“for all past eternity
“and now and into all eternity.
Amen.”
Well, we know Jehovah had no beginning.
We have a hard time grasping that.
When Jehovah was alone before he created the Logos,
there was no change, because Jehovah does not change.
This helps us to understand in what way Jehovah always existed.
Jehovah is not subject to time.
He exists independently and outside
from what we perceive as time.
Where the New World Translation
translates “past eternity,” in Jude 25,
the Greek original text
says “before all time.”
Surprise, surprise—before time.
The conclusion is that time had a beginning.
Is this a new understanding? No.
If you want to put down a reference,
Watchtower, 1982, September 1—
September 1, page 22, and paragraph 17.
It says about this verse in Jude 25:
“Jude appropriately ascribed glory, majesty,
“might and authority to Jehovah
‘for all past eternity,’”
or to quote The Watchtower,
“‘before all time,’
as men might know it.”
We seem safe to say
that time as we know it, as humans,
came into being when Jehovah
started to create first the Logos.
But what we perceive as time now
will continue forever and ever in the future.
At 1 Corinthians 7:29, it says:
“Moreover, this I say, brothers, the time left is reduced.”
Christ had given his disciples
the sign of his presence and had warned them:
“Keep on the watch, therefore, because you do not know
on what day your Lord is coming.”
—Matthew 24:3, 42.
The time left was “reduced”
in the sense that those first-century Christians
had to live constantly in expectation of Christ’s coming.
Furthermore, they did not know
how much time remained for them individually
before “time and unforeseen occurrence”
brought their life to a close.
As an important event nears, there’s an increased sense of urgency.
How can we illustrate that?
Well, suppose there’s a wedding.
The days before are very busy in order to prepare well for the event.
Even on the wedding day, the bride will be urgently preparing herself
so the wedding party does not have to wait,
which would be very impolite.
If you have to catch a flight,
you are perhaps urgently and nervously preparing your luggage,
making sure that you are at the airport on time
because you do not want to miss the flight.
Suppose a farmer has a mature crop ready to be harvested.
Suddenly, there is a storm warning.
Dark clouds loom at the horizon.
The storm could destroy the crop.
Don’t you think that he’ll urgently organize
his whole household to go out to the field
and begin to bring in the crop
before the storm hits?
Christians are involved in a harvesting work.
John 4:35 quotes Jesus, saying:
‘View the fields, that they are ripe for harvesting.’
The harvest time will soon be over.
So are we making good use of our time
to help bring in the harvest?
“The harvest is great, but the workers are few,”
said Jesus.—Matthew 9:37.
And that shows the urgency.
The hurricane of the great tribulation is close!
It’s a hurricane in the illustration, so we need to hurry.
When a woman is close to giving birth
and the birth pangs started —the water broke, let’s say—
then it is urgent to rush her to the hospital
or call a midwife to come to the home.
Jesus’ death was a much more important event
than a wedding, a birth, a flight, or a crop.
As the appointed time for Jesus’ sacrificial death
drew near, his sense of urgency increased.
Jesus stepped up his activity and his preaching
as the time for him to be on earth ran out.
True Christians have always lived with a sense of urgency.
In the first century, Christians in Judea and Jerusalem
needed to “keep on the watch,”
and that was imperative because Jesus warned
that the Roman armies would come and would attack the city.
And he said:
“Let those in Judea begin fleeing to the mountains.”
It was urgent!
Now more than ever, the time that remains
before Jehovah destroys false religion
through political elements is reduced.
It is vital, then, that we make
wise use of our time —the time that remains.
How?
As the apostle Paul explains in Ephesians 5:16,
we must ‘buy out the opportune time’ for “the more important things”
at the expense of what is nonessential.
We need to make every day count.
Do we live as though the end could come at any time,
or do we live as though it is far off?
Jesus warned:
“The Son of man is coming at an hour that you
do not think to be it.” —Matthew 24:44.
Our pattern of life reflects how much we trust in Jehovah
by putting faith in his prophetic Word,
keeping the urgency of the times in mind.
Avoid a complacent attitude,
like the people of Sodom and Gomorrah had.
‘They were eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building,’ said Jesus.
‘But on the day that Lot came out of Sodom,
‘it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all.’
It was urgent for Lot and his family to flee,
and it’s urgent for us too.
We need to be prepared.
We can prepare, for instance, if we live in an earthquake zone
by having our houses built earthquake-proof.
It costs more
—more effort, more time involved preparing the house—
but when an earthquake hits,
then we are better prepared to survive.
Revelation refers to “the four angels who”
have prepared the hour,
or “have been prepared for the hour and day and month and year,”
units of time that we can understand. —Revelation 9:14, 15.
Seeing how prophecies were fulfilled at specific times
should inspire faith in the God of “times and seasons”
and in his Word.
Soon the angels will let loose the four winds of destruction.
Are we ready?
Jehovah is a perfect Timekeeper.
Do we make good use of what we perceive as time
by attending meetings, reading the Bible daily
—even after Gilead graduation—
going out in field ministry?
Whereas, it is appropriate to take time for leisure and other activities,
it is good not to waste time
but keep the balance.
If we use time wisely
—buying it out by giving priority to spiritual things
and sacrifice less important time as a payment, so to say—
then we will see the promise fulfilled
to live forever and ever and ever.
No more need, then, to worry about time.
But now is the time to conclude my talk,
so I would not go overtime.
Thank you very much, Brother Lösch.
We thoroughly enjoyed that,
and we appreciate your hard work and meditation.
Now, we’ll share some greetings
from various branches
and highlight some of the things
that they wanted to pass on.
Angola: “With their faith strengthened by means of a thorough study of God’s Word
“and refined spiritual qualities, the graduates will give a fine contribution
to further stabilize and strengthen Jehovah’s organization.”
Then Argentina:
“Although the school of Gilead
“will soon become a memory
[they didn’t know about Brother Herd’s talk]
you will treasure it for the rest of your lives.”
Armenia: “We rejoice with you graduates on this special day.
“We’re delighted to see how Jehovah is training
more brothers and sisters to take on additional responsibility.”
Benin: You’ll find this one quite interesting.
This part I’ll pass on.
“To all of you [and this is to the students, or graduates]
“Please, hurry up!
We are waiting for you out here in the worldwide field.”
Bolivia: “Our hearts rejoice along with you, dear Gilead graduates,
on this day that brings so much praise to our heavenly Father.”
And then Britain: “What a wonderful blessing
“and unique privilege it is for each student to have
his or her faith strengthened through an intensive study of God’s Word.”
Burundi: “The five months of Bible training that you have received
“will give added impetus to the all-important work
of helping all who are ‘rightly disposed for everlasting life.’”
And then Congo (Kinshasa): “We ‘rejoice with those who rejoice.’
This is, indeed, a special day for all the graduates.”
Georgia, the country: “Congratulations
on successfully completing the spiritually enriching course of study.”
Germany: “Please accept warm love and greetings
“from Selters Bethel in Germany!
“Jehovah, as our Grand Instructor,
continues to educate his servants in a wonderful way.”
Haiti: “This graduation is another proof that Jehovah
does treat his loyal servants in a ‘special way.’”
And then France: “We wish to send you
“the very warm love from the France Bethel family
as you are about to receive your diplomas along with your service assignments.”
And Japan sends their “warm Christian love and greetings.
All graduates must have experienced firsthand Jehovah’s loving care.”
Kenya: “As you now take the benefit
“of this training with you to your assignments,
we are confident that ‘Jehovah will be with you wherever you go.’”
The Netherlands: “Please accept our warm love and greetings,
“and may Jehovah continue to bless you in your assignment,
whether a new one or one you are familiar with.”
Nigeria sends their “warmest greetings to all.”
Paraguay passes on their wish to have
‘Jehovah bless all your efforts in training.’
Solomon Islands, known as the Happy Isles,
wishes to send their “warmest Christian love and greetings.”
Suriname: This is quite interesting.
They share this point:
“In 1959, two brothers from Suriname
“attended the 32nd class of Gilead.
“Since then, many in Suriname nurtured the dream of going to Gilead.
“Now, 57 years later,
we rejoice with the privilege of having one more student attending a class.”
And then Thailand:
“From the Land of Smiles, we add our happy smiles
to yours and send our warm love and greetings to all on this special day.”
And finally, Ukraine:
“During the past five months, the Great Potter, Jehovah God,
“was intensely molding you so that you can now say:
“‘We are all the clay, and you are our Potter;
we are all the work of your hand.’”
So we appreciate those sincere greetings
from our brothers throughout the earth.
Now, before we share
the diplomas with you,
we want to just pass on these statistics.
The brothers like to receive these.
For this particular 141st class:
number of single brothers, 12;
number of single sisters, 4;
number of married couples, 16;
total number of students, 48;
their average age, 40.8;
average years in the truth, 25.1;
average years in full-time ministry, 19.0.
So for those that love statistics,
you now have them.
Now, we’re going to have the presentation
of the diplomas to the 141st class of Gilead.
Brother David Schafer is going to help me.
He’s a helper to the Teaching Committee,
and he’ll be helping as we
pass on the diplomas
to these graduates of the 141st class of Gilead.
So let’s take a look at them.
So, first, we have Brother and Sister Barnizo,
who will be returning to the Philippines.
Brother Bingen will be returning to Suriname.
Brother Bockstaele will be serving in the Solomon Islands.
Brother Burchall will be returning to Liberia.
Brother Cano will be returning to Argentina.
Brother and Sister Cook will be returning to Britain.
Brother and Sister Ernits will be returning to Estonia.
Brother and Sister Fais will be returning to Italy.
Sister Gaši will be returning to Serbia.
Brother and Sister Gewitz will be returning to Denmark.
Brother and Sister Gustave will be returning to France.
Brother and Sister Janian will be serving in Georgia.
Brother and Sister Karapetyan will be returning to Armenia.
Brother and Sister Kreuger will be returning to the Netherlands.
Brother Lobo will be returning to Chile.
Brother Mamulashvili will be returning to Georgia.
Brother and Sister Martinez will be returning to Paraguay.
Brother and Sister Mbanzulu will be returning to Congo (Kinshasa).
Brother and Sister Onyango will be returning to Kenya.
Sister Paillard will be returning to Asia.
Brother Pritchard will be serving in Benin.
Brother and Sister Rosenzvig will be returning to Israel.
Brother and Sister Ryan will be returning to Ghana.
Sister Schumi will be returning to Asia.
Brother Steiner will be returning to Germany.
Brother Titus will be returning to Papua New Guinea.
Brother and Sister Ungebaev will be returning to Finland.
Brother Vetlovas will be returning to Lithuania.
Brother Wafula will be returning to Kenya.
Sister Xayalad will be returning to Asia.
Brother Yagotintsev will be returning to Russia.
And Brother and Sister Yiga will be returning to Uganda.
So at this point, as we customarily do,
we’re going to have the class resolution letter read,
and Brother Richard Cook will do that for the class.
“To the Governing Body and the Bethel family.
“Dear Brothers:
“From the moment we received our invitations to Gilead
“down to this day of graduation,
“we feel we have received a gift of undeserved kindness
“from Jehovah and his organization.
“There is nothing that we have done or could ever do
“to deserve the instruction, training, molding,
“and loving attention that we have received over the past five months.
“Just as Isaiah 26:12 says:
“‘O Jehovah, . . .
“everything we have done you have accomplished for us.’
“Jehovah has given us the privilege
“of experiencing close association
“with you dear brothers of the Governing Body.
“Your humility, your love for the brotherhood,
“and your absolute determination
“to follow Jehovah’s direction have deeply impressed us.
“We saw this clearly during your faith-strengthening lectures
“but also in the lighter moments
“that you shared with us outside of the classroom,
“all the while preparing for your move to Warwick.
“Seeing your examples firsthand has only made us more convinced
“that this is the organization
“Jehovah is blessing and directing today.
“What a true joy it has been for us
“to be part of this delightful Bethel family!
“You’ve been an example in hospitality,
“making us feel at home away from home.
“The excellent work of so many departments has created an environment
“where studying day and night and night and day
“was both possible and enjoyable.
“An essential part of our learning experience
“has been seeing the faith
“of so many of you long-time members of the family.
“We have also learned from the faith of you,
“the many commuters and temporary volunteers,
“who willingly make yourselves available
“to serve here at Bethel.
“We are truly grateful to you, our dear instructors,
“for generously giving of your very selves,
“both mind and heart,
“in the way that you have taught us.
“During our training, your love for the Bible truth
“that you were teaching touched us deeply.
“Your accuracy and yet your warmth,
“your seriousness and yet your humor
“showed us a balance worthy of imitation.
“Your obvious determination to hold fast to the direction
“of ‘the faithful and discreet slave’
“has made a lasting impression on us.
“As we go to our assignments, we are resolved to do
“as 1 Peter 4:10 states:
“‘To the extent that each one has received a gift,
“‘use it in ministering to one another
“as fine stewards of God’s undeserved kindness.’
“Gilead has been a priceless gift
“from Jehovah through all of you.
“Having been shown such undeserved kindness,
“we desire to use it to demonstrate our love for Jehovah.
“More than ever before, we are determined to continue
“to advance the preaching of the good news and to strengthen our brothers.
“It is our earnest prayer that this be our life’s work,
“all to the honor and glory of our heavenly Father, Jehovah.
Your brothers and sisters of the 141st class of Gilead.”
Before we have a brief moment
for some concluding comments, I have some more statistics.
But this is of interest to us with the attendance figures:
Canada, 679;
the United States, that’s 9,814.
But this is who that includes:
Patterson, 3,519;
Brooklyn, 1,405;
Fishkill, 763;
Wallkill, 2,540;
Warwick, 1,219;
Curaçao, 61;
Fort Lauderdale, Florida, 134;
Jamaica, 37; and Puerto Rico, 136.
So that makes a grand total of 10,493.
I don’t know what the delay was for,
but they all know hundreds of thousands
are going to see it pretty soon.
And that’s really what I wanted to just pass on to you.
Just a brief review of some of the key thoughts,
and we certainly can’t touch on all of it.
But “See—The Cloud!”
Follow the cloud, not men— nice reminder.
And of course, you’ll always remember Brother Herd’s talk,
and nice thought, “Smells ring bells.”
Again, the translators will have fun with that.
And then the warning about ego; it’s a good caution, counsel.
And nice thoughts about testing Jehovah and being tested.
And, of course, all the good experiences and interviews
and Brother Lösch reminding us to make good use of our time.
So it’s been a wonderful program.
What’s nice, too, because you get into your assignment
and because Jehovah has blessed us with the broadcasting of the program
—so that will be up there in due course—
and now this has been permeating
with excitement with your family and close friends.
And see now,
with Jehovah’s blessing on this project,
you can go and play it months from now.
You might face some discouraging circumstance.
Well, go back, and you can stop it
—think about it.
I mean, what a blessing, especially for you graduates
to be able to go back and then just absorb more.
So keep that in mind, and Jehovah will bless you
with good, good reminders in the days ahead.
So at this point, we’re going to invite all—
Now, we were supposed to all be ready to sing this new song,
and I know my wife and I practiced.
We hope you practiced.
Those that know how to read music,
please sing out and help those around you.
It’s a beautiful song, and I love the lyrics now.
See, because we’ve had—
One of my favorites is song 135 in the songbook we have at this point.
But see, this has a message here,
and you sing and you keep this in mind in your assignment:
“We Will,” not might,
“We Will Keep Enduring.”
So take these lyrics to heart as you go to your assignments.
So let’s stand and sing song number 154.
And then Brother Leon Weaver,
a helper to the Service Committee of the Governing Body,
will conclude with prayer.

titles.ko: 제141기 길르앗 졸업식: 3부—결론 연설 및 임명
titles.en: 141st Gilead Graduation: Part 3—Concluding Talk and Assignments
titles.cn: 第141届基列学校毕业典礼：第3部分（最后演讲与委派）

en.text: We always enjoy this part at our Gilead graduations
—the student experiences that they’ve had
from the field activity while they were at school.
Kenneth Olson, an instructor
with Theocratic Schools Department, will handle this part.
And they have the theme “The Scene of This World Is Changing.”
The apostle Paul once wrote to the congregation in Corinth:
“The scene of this world is changing.” (1Co 7:31)
And in doing so, he likened the world to a stage
with actors playing their various roles until a change of scenes.
So surrounded by the potential distractions
of the world there in the first century,
our brothers needed to give priority to spiritual matters.
True worship had to come first.
And an important way they showed that they kept their spiritual focus
was through their obedience to Jesus’ command to preach and teach.
And they did this in various ways.
Notice the example of the apostle Paul
at Acts 17:17.
There in Acts 17:17, it says:
“So he began to reason in the synagogue with the Jews
“and the other people who worshipped God
“and every day in the marketplace
with those who happened to be on hand.”
So we notice that Paul, in the marketplace,
was ready to talk to whoever happened to be on hand.
Now, he didn’t know who they would be, but he was ready.
So the principles that apply then,
apply now because many of the concerns
that people had back then, people have now.
And so our work is like it was in the first century.
Now, as Brother and Sister Cook were traveling to Gilead School,
they, like Paul, were ready.
They were alert to speak with those who happened to be on hand.
This time, it was not in the marketplace; it was at a train station.
And notice how they were ready to discuss various topics
as we watch this video reenactment.
Thank you so much, Manny, for helping us with the bags.
We really appreciate that.
Well, you certainly have a lot of bags.
Where are you going?
We are going to Patterson, New York,
to attend a Bible school for the next six months.
Really? A six-month Bible school?
Wow, that is amazing!
Yeah, we’re Jehovah’s Witnesses, Manny.
I’m sure you’ve heard about us.
There’s our little card.
Yeah, I have seen Jehovah’s Witnesses going from door to door.
You even go out when the weather is really cold.
I have a lot of respect for you people.
Oh, thank you.
Well, we love sharing the Bible message with people.
Here, Manny, on the back of this tract, there’s a QR Code
and it takes you to our website, jw.org.
So on there, there are publications you can download and read,
but also there’s a section that answers questions you might have about the Bible.
Hmm, that’s good. I have some questions.
In fact, my mother died last year.
She suffered for such a long time.
Oh, sorry.
So sorry to hear that.
We’re very sorry.
Losing someone dear must be so difficult.
Yeah, well, it kind of affected my faith.
You know, she was a wonderful person.
Why did she have to suffer like that?
I can understand you feeling that way, Manny.
When you’ve lived a life like your mom, and she’s been such a good person,
and then she suffers like that, I mean, it’s— it’s difficult to bear, isn’t it?
It’s difficult to bear.
This tract, it’s asking the question: “Will Suffering Ever End?”
Do you think that’s the sort of question you’re really asking?
Yes, it is.
Well, thank you. Thank you very much.
You know, I can stay with you until your friend comes for you. That’s OK?
Oh, will you?
Oh, thank you!
Thank you!
Thank you very much!
I’ve been thinking about this.
You know, the whole world is a mess.
We agree with you.
But why is it a mess?
I can show you another tract.
It does have an interesting question.
It says, “Who Really Controls the World?”
And you will be surprised to know the answer.
Notice what the Bible says:
“The Evil One controls the whole world.”
So did you notice who is in control?
What does the Bible say?
Hmm. It says the Evil One —means the Devil?
That’s right.
Well, that explains why the world is in such a bad condition.
Uh-huh.
And you know, Manny, the Bible says that God has set up a kingdom
that is going to overrule the Devil,
and also He is going to bring the suffering to an end.
Oh, may I have that tract as well?
Of course, yeah, this is for you.
I just wanted to point on the back again in this tract
is our website that Richard just mentioned.
If you would like, you can go there,
and you can ask for somebody to come and visit you,
and you can discuss all the questions you have,
and they will answer you from the Bible.
Oh, well, thank you very much. Thank you.
You are welcome.
Excuse me, Brother and Sister Cook?
Oh, this is our driver!
Yes, pleased to meet you!
Nice to meet you.
Thank you for collecting us.
Here are their bags. Thank you.
Thank you.
Well, it was a pleasure meeting you.
Thank you.
Thank you, Manny. We really appreciate all your help.
Thank you for your help.
Bye-bye.
Goodbye.
Take care.
So, hope you had a good trip coming here.
Yeah, it was really good.
So, did you see how Brother and Sister Cook were prepared?
They had literature ready.
They didn’t know who it would be or what the topic would be,
but they were ready.
Another way that our first-century brothers and sisters obeyed Jesus’ command
is found at Acts 5:42.
At Acts 5:42,
it says there:
“And every day in the temple and from house to house
“they continued without letup
“teaching and declaring the good news
about the Christ, Jesus.”
So it says they went “from house to house.”
Now, this was shortly after Pentecost of 33 C.E.,
and already the young congregation is active in the door-to-door ministry,
talking to people face-to-face.
And this work is still at the center —it’s at the forefront—
of our worldwide preaching effort.
So contacting people directly
helps us to help them individually.
Now, in the first century, Jesus helped people face-to-face,
very often with the resurrection hope.
He built them up; he gave them hope.
Now we do the same.
However, very often, when we talk to people from house to house,
we’re there, we have a scripture, we’re prepared,
we have a topic we want to talk about.
And all of a sudden, the householder wants
to talk about what’s on their mind and heart.
Essentially, they change the subject.
So, what do we do?
Well, an alert teacher will follow
the concern of the householder and address that concern.
So watch how Brother Mbanzulu
followed the householder’s concern
and comforted him with the resurrection hope
when he was invited into a man’s home for the very first time.
And see how he changed the subject, and Brother Mbanzulu followed it.
Thank you for inviting us in.
You’re welcome.
How would you describe the situation in the world today?
I lost my wife a few years ago,
and life is not easy.
We are so sorry to hear that you lost your wife.
That must be difficult to deal with.
It is difficult.
But I know you’re going to say that I should be—
there’s the hope of the resurrection
and that with a little bit of money, I’ll be able to see my wife again.
But I don’t know if I believe that.
Did someone say to you that you need to pay something
like money to see your wife again?
Yes, that’s what the church said.
Oh, I’m so sorry to hear that.
But really, do you believe that God needs our money?
Of course not!
But I don’t believe that the resurrection is true.
What is your point of view?
Where do we come from?
I guess, of course,
there had to be some person that made us.
Life just couldn’t come about by itself.
So I would say that person is God.
So let me give you an example.
Suppose that you own a company that makes cars.
Let’s say you make Mercedes-Benz,
and you decide to give a new one to your friend.
He’s very happy.
But the very first day he drives that car, he has a crash.
Then he calls you; he’s sad; he says,
“You know, I just had a crash.”
What will you say?
Just bring it back. I’ll fix it.
But what if he said to you:
“Friend, I’m not sure you will fix it.
It’s totally broken.”
What will you say to him?
If I made it, I can fix it.
I could even make a new one.
You know, when something does not work properly in our body,
or let’s say, when our body stops working,
we call it death.
But actually, from the point of view
of the One who created life, we can say this is just like a crash.
Would you agree with that?
Yeah, I would agree with that.
And when this happens, usually we are very sad
because that person that died
may be someone we really loved.
But could the One who created life
be able to fix the problem
or recreate that person?
Yeah, He should be able to do that.
But you know, we three here,
we’ve never seen someone raised from the dead.
So talking about the resurrection
must be something strange to us.
And God understands that.
But you know what Jesus said in the past when he was here on earth?
He said something very interesting, and I would like to share it with you.
It’s found in the book of John,
chapter 5, verses 28 and 29.
And while Sulamite is reading that scripture,
please try to imagine that God is speaking to you personally.
Please Sula, can you read it?
Uh-huh.
“Do not be amazed at this,
“for the hour is coming in which all those in the memorial tombs
“will hear his voice and come out,
“those who did good things to a resurrection of life,
and those who practiced vile things to a resurrection of judgment.”
God knows that may look impossible to you,
but he assures us that this will take place.
It’s clear now.
You know, there are many other good promises
in the Bible from God for humankind.
And if you want, we can help you to know them.
Yeah, I would like that.
Did you see how Brother Mbanzulu was willing
to drop the topic he wanted to talk about
and follow the concern of the man instead?
Very loving and very alert.
Now, in the first century,
there were many different ideas and philosophies of life.
Pontius Pilate expressed one when he said to Jesus:
“What is truth?”
And he said that rather scornfully.
But today some feel unsure
if it’s possible to know truth.
Well, our first-century brothers
would often find common ground with someone,
to reason with them and help them see the point.
And we do the same today.
Watch how Sister Martinez found common ground
to reason with a man who seemed unsure
if it were possible to know truth.
Good morning, Sir.
Good morning.
I’m glad to find you here,
and we’re asking people in the area a question,
and I’d like your opinion.
OK, sure.
Do you think that it’s actually possible
for us to get to know what the truth is,
living in a world where more half-truths exist?
No, I don’t think so. Nobody has the truth.
I’m sure you have your own religion and, in fact,
your own translation of the Bible.
And everyone’s entitled
to believe what they want to believe.
Yeah, we all have the right to believe
in what we want to believe in.
But do you think that God
wants us to get to know what the truth is?
Hmm, yeah, sure.
You know, I noticed that you have an accent.
If you don’t mind me asking, where are you from?
Oh, I don’t mind. I’m from Ecuador.
Oh! Wow!
You know, I’ve been living in South America
for the past few years with my husband.
Oh, really? What country?
In Paraguay.
Oh, yeah. OK, I know Paraguay. Nice.
Yeah, you know, they speak Spanish there also,
and they have a little bit of an accent.
Uh-huh.
They also use certain expressions
that are unfamiliar to me.
But, generally, I can understand what they’re saying.
True, it is slightly different. Mhm.
This reminds me of when we study the Bible.
For example, the translation that we use,
they’re in many languages.
The Bible that we have in Spanish
wasn’t originally in Spanish.
It’s a translation.
Uh-huh. Right.
And although one Bible may differ slightly from another,
even within the same language,
they generally convey the same idea.
Hmm. Yeah, that makes sense. Sure.
Now, do you think that God is aware
of these apparent difficulties that exist?
Hmm. Good question. Yeah, I think so.
Yeah, he definitely has to know.
And, you know, he actually encourages us
through the Bible to get to know what these truths are.
Hmm.
These truths are revealed clearly here
in this Bible text
at 1 Timothy 2:3,4 that I’d like to read to you.
It says: “This is fine and acceptable
“in the sight of our Savior, God,
“whose will is that all sorts of people should be saved and,”
notice this part,
“come to an accurate knowledge of truth.”
Hmm. OK.
Not half-truths.
Right.
So God is really concerned about us
coming to an accurate knowledge of truth.
Now, do you think that this is possible
if we dedicate time
researching the Bible on a superficial level?
No, I don’t think so.
You can’t come to accurate knowledge like that.
It’s impossible.
Yeah, I think the same way.
It really means that we have to investigate
in what God is trying to tell us in such a large book.
Hmm.
You know, I have this book with me
that has this very interesting theme
“What Does the Bible Really Teach?”
Hmm. Sounds interesting.
And it reveals what those Bible truths are.
I would like to get this available to you.
I only have it in English.
OK.
How can I do this?
Well, I have to leave now.
I have to go to work, but I’ll give you my contact information,
and then we can make arrangements.
Oh, that sounds great.
Yeah.
OK.
OK.
No doubt you saw how Sister Martinez was able to use
things that they had in common
to help the man reason about the point.
Now, we’ve seen so far, students preaching in the train station,
peoples’ homes, a parking lot.
Well, really, Jesus set the example
about reaching people wherever they may be.
Notice in Matthew 9:9,
there in Matthew 9:9,
it says there:
“Next, while moving on from there,
“Jesus caught sight of a man named Matthew
“sitting at the tax office,
“and he said to him: ‘Be my follower.’
At that he rose up and followed him.”
So Matthew was sitting at the tax office.
He was in his place of employment.
So Jesus preached in business territory.
Well, we do the same thing today.
We preach in business territory.
We try to reach people where they are.
Now, back in the first century,
we know the main theme was the Kingdom.
This was the theme of the preaching work.
This is still the case today.
This is the theme of the preaching work.
In our last reenactment, it takes place in a beauty salon.
Our sister is coming back to the woman’s place of business
in order to cultivate the interest shown in the very first conversation,
and notice how she directs attention to the Kingdom.
Hi, Deanne!
Hi!
It’s so nice to see you again.
Today I brought a video to show you.
It’s called Does God Have a Name?
Does God have a name?
. . . at a time and place convenient for you.
So as you saw in the video,
we all have names to identify ourselves.
Your name is Deanne, and my name is Claire.
So wouldn’t it make sense for God to have a name to identify himself with?
Sure, that makes perfect sense.
And did you know that the name Jehovah is in the Bible about 7,000 times?
Wow!
If it’s in there that much, it must be important.
You know, Claire, I do read the Bible every day.
And I’ve been trying to get closer to God,
but it’s not easy.
You know, I’m so busy running the business
and looking after my children.
And that’s another thing, I’m constantly worried about my children.
The world is just getting so bad.
I wonder about their future.
Yeah, I can imagine that it’s not easy.
But it’s good that you’re looking to the Bible.
In fact, today I wanted to show you a verse
from Daniel 2:44,
it says:
“In the days of those kings the God of heaven
“will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.
“And this kingdom will not be passed on to any other people.
“It will crush and put an end to all these kingdoms,
and it alone will stand forever.”
Perhaps you’ve heard of people pray the Our Father,
and they’re asking for God’s Kingdom to come.
They want to see God’s will done
on the earth as it was in heaven.
And really, that’s what this Kingdom is talking about.
It’s God’s government to bring an end to suffering in the world.
I would really like to see that change.
Yeah, we all want to see an end to suffering.
But what do you think?
Do you think God really has the power to bring about these changes?
Of course! I think he has all the power.
Yeah, that’s right, he does.
And, you know, he also wants
to see an end to this suffering.
In fact, that’s why it’s so important for us
to try and learn as much as we can about his purpose for the earth.
I would like to learn more about God
and what he’s going to do for the future.
Yeah, that’s so good.
I really enjoy speaking to you about this.
I was thinking, do you usually work here on Saturday mornings?
I do. I work here just about every Saturday.
So if you come, we can sit down for a few minutes and talk.
Oh, I would really appreciate if we can have a little bit
of time together to talk about that subject.
Sure.
Thank you so much. It was nice to see you today.
You too.
Bye-bye.
Bye-bye.
Our Gilead students have been doing a very good job
directing people to the Kingdom
as the only true hope for mankind.
Now, in the first century,
our brothers and sisters faced
many of the challenges that are common today.
How should they view higher education,
how to keep focused on spiritual goals,
how to avoid the dangers of bad association?
Well, our Gilead students have faced these very issues successfully.
And the decisions that they’ve made in the past
have helped them be here today.
Now notice how our students met the various challenges posed
by what to do with higher education,
potential distractions from their spiritual goals,
and avoiding bad associations.
Would you like to meet some of our Gilead students
and get to know them just a little bit better?
Well, we have with us Brother and Sister Mbanzulu,
Fall and Sulamite Mbanzulu, from Congo Kinshasa.
We have Brother Elipaz and Nancy Rosenzvig, from Israel,
and Sister Turkijana Gasi, from Serbia.
And we’re glad to have all of you with us.
Brother Mbanzulu, let’s start with you.
What spiritual goal did you set for yourself as you were growing up?
I wanted to be a special pioneer.
Well, that’s an excellent spiritual goal for a young man.
Now as that— Once you set that goal, however,
a potential obstacle arose.
Yes, this happened when I was 14 years old.
My father said to me that he would support me financially
and even pay for my education
if I would like to be a lawyer or a physician.
So he offered you free higher education.
Yeah.
But you had this other spiritual goal in mind.
Yeah.
What did you do?
I kindly explained to him that I had the goal to be
a special pioneer, so I declined his offer.
Well, that sounds like a good thing.
You kept your focus on spiritual matters.
What did your father think about that?
He was very disappointed
because he didn’t expect that answer.
He said to me if I did not take his offer,
I will have to support myself.
And if, in the future, I have to face some difficulties,
I should not go back to him.
And he even mentioned that I was no longer his son,
and that hurt me deeply.
But I’m happy that I made that decision,
because otherwise I would not have benefited
from the highest education
—the divine education that I’ve enjoyed in Gilead.
Well, we know that was not an easy situation
to face as a young man
—quite a lot of faith and spiritual focus—
and we’re glad that you did that.
So you went ahead with your goal to special pioneer.
So when did you become a special pioneer?
I never did.
What happened?
I was invited to serve in Bethel, and I accepted that invitation.
Well, we know that Jehovah’s blessed you there too.
Yeah, I received many blessings in Bethel,
and one of them, actually, is my marriage
with Sulamite.
It’s really a gift coming from Jehovah.
And Sulamite loves Jehovah and supports me in my service.
Yes.
Well, Sister Mbanzulu, now, your father was Muslim.
Yes.
And what did he think about the family being Jehovah’s Witnesses?
My father never opposed the truth.
He saw that this was good and even encouraged us.
All right. So that allowed you to set spiritual goals.
Yes.
What spiritual goal did you set for yourself?
I wanted to be a special pioneer.
That’s an excellent spiritual goal!
And what did your family think about that goal?
My immediate family was supportive.
But others in the family pressured me to pursue
higher education and travel to Europe.
That could have been a temptation, but it was a trap.
Spiritual education is far more valuable.
I’m glad I made a good decision —the right choice.
Well, so we’re glad too.
So both of you had to stay spiritually focused there.
So you went ahead with your goal of being a special pioneer.
When did you become a special pioneer?
I didn’t become a special pioneer.
I was invited to serve at Bethel for two weeks,
and then I was invited to stay in Bethel service.
Well, that’s good.
You both remained focused on spiritual goals
but flexible to Jehovah’s direction,
and we’re glad that you did.
Brother Rosenzvig,
now, you come from a very spiritually active family.
What did your parents do to raise you
in such a fine spiritual environment?
It’s true, today when I’m looking back,
I see that my parents did so much.
In addition to our family study,
my parents studied with all five of us separately.
They went with us to service;
we read together the daily text.
And also my father,
he prayed with each one of us every night.
So, what influence did all that have on your spiritual routine?
So I still pray every night with my wife.
And recently, I asked my brothers and sisters
if they have the same habit until today.
And all of them said, “Yes.”
So all of us pray every night like we did with our father.
Excellent.
Well, I know that you met a spiritually-minded sister
in your congregation; you got married.
And then what did you do to make yourself more available
to pursue spiritual goals?
So we began to simplify our life,
we avoided financial obligation,
and we expanded our ministry.
After a while, we were invited to Bethel.
Well, that’s excellent —wonderful invitation.
I’m sure you were very excited.
Now, when that happened, though,
a potential distraction arose.
Yeah, my employer, he really wanted me to stay.
So he offered me a big raise,
stock in the company, a car.
But the real riches are found in the full-time service.
And look!
Here we are, getting the divine education that Jehovah provides.
Yeah, very true.
Now Sister Rosenzvig, so when your husband received
the invitation to Bethel, obviously it’s to you too,
and you also had some potential distractions come at the same time.
True.
The same week we were invited to Bethel,
I got a phone call from a company that offered me a well-paying job.
And just before that, I had said no to a full scholarship
to pursue more education.
And both of us got so many offers during that time,
it was very clear somebody was not happy about our decision.
Yes.
Now your first name,
Sister Rosenzvig, doesn’t sound very Israeli.
How did you come to be called Nancy?
So my father is from an Arabic background
and my mom from a Jewish background.
As you know, in Israel, it’s not so common
for a Jew to marry an Arab.
But this is what’s so beautiful about our organization.
And the brothers and sisters in Israel
really give a good witness in this regard.
But still my parents decided to make both sides
of the family happy and gave me an American name.
That’s very diplomatic of them.
And how did your parents help you
to have a spiritual environment
in which you could set good spiritual goals?
Both of my parents are really good students of the Bible.
And I would always see them prepare for the meeting,
and we would never miss a meeting without a good reason.
Additionally, my mom,
before she got married, she was a special pioneer.
Both her and my dad, they loved talking about Jehovah
and going out in the ministry.
I know that your mother also made considerable effort
to cultivate your love for the ministry.
Yes.
There is one experience I really remember.
I was very young.
She took me to preach in unassigned territory
in a city near Mount Hermon, and we preached for some hours.
And after that, she took me to eat my favorite food
—hummus and french fries.
Ah, and how has their example influenced you until today?
Until today, I have good study habits,
I have deep appreciation for our meetings,
and I love talking about Jehovah.
And I still like hummus and french fries.
Now, when you were in school,
you were different from all of the other children.
All of the other children were Jewish.
And we know that as a young person, it can be especially difficult
to be different from everyone else.
How did you handle that?
For a while, I found it difficult to speak about my religion at school,
but then I thought to myself, ‘I need to be proud
that I am one of Jehovah’s Witnesses.’
So I just decided to speak with one of my classmates.
And when I told her, she said,
“Oh, now I understand why you are so different.”
And the conversation went so well.
I felt relief, and things were much easier at school after that.
So, what advice would you have for young people who are in school today?
I would say: “Just be proud that you are one of Jehovah’s Witnesses.
“We are serving the best God,
“and tell your classmates about it as soon as possible.
“That will make you happy, and more important,
it will make Jehovah happy, and he will bless your efforts.”
Yes.
Sister Gasi.
Sister Gasi, you serve in Serbia,
you live there, but you didn’t grow up there.
No, I was born in Kosovo.
I grew up in the Roma culture with the Muslim background.
All right.
I know that your father is fairly well-known in the Roma community,
and there are some deeply held traditions
that had an impact on you concerning your schooling.
Yeah, culturally among the Roma people it was expected
that the oldest girl stop going to school when she is quite young.
So my father wanted me to stop going to school.
And honestly, I was very unhappy because of that
because I really loved going to school.
So I explained— I told my father
that I will respect his decision,
but also I took the opportunity to explain to him
that I wanted to pioneer.
I explained to him what it means, and he agreed.
Well, that was very good.
So you respected your father’s wishes
but also clearly set out your spiritual goals.
We’re glad he supported you in that.
But now that you’re out preaching in the town
that must have called attention.
Yes. A neighbor approached my father about it,
and he said: “You’re Muslim.
Why do you allow your daughter to go house to house?”
And my father told him
he never had a problem with his girls
since they started to study the Bible.
Well, your good conduct spoke out there.
Now, we know that, unfortunately, war broke out in the region
and Kosovo was affected.
And at that time, there were no brothers in the area,
there was no congregation, no meetings.
And even your father and brothers
were not there at that time,
leaving you, your sister, and your mother
to rely on Jehovah there.
And we know Jehovah can do that, but that can be very stressful.
But there was an additional situation that arose.
Tell us about that.
Our neighbor had a basement in his house,
and many of us —where our area was bombed—
many of us took shelter there.
Physically it was safe,
but people talked about how we were going to die
and about the horrible things that could happen to us,
and it was very discouraging to listen to that.
I realized that it was bad association.
I had to make a change to keep spiritually alive.
All right.
So you had the basement which served as a bomb shelter
giving physical security, but it came with bad association.
So you said you had to make a change.
What did you do?
We stayed home,
we read the experiences from the yearbook,
we held the meetings in our kitchen,
and also we read
and studied the Bible, we prayed together.
This built up our faith, and Jehovah helped us to endure.
And what has been the result?
Jehovah has given me the best school here at Gilead
and also the best association with my fellow classmates.
Well, we thank all of you for sharing some of your experiences involving decisions
that helped you be here today with Jehovah’s blessing.
Well, the scene of the world is changing,
but our faithfulness to Jehovah remains steadfast.
May Jehovah continue to bless the students
of the 141st class of Gilead
and the entire worldwide brotherhood
as we work shoulder to shoulder to Jehovah’s praise.
Thank you very much.
We always enjoy the experiences in the field
as well as their personal experiences.
Next, Brother Ronald Curzan, a helper to the Teaching Committee,
is going to interview others from the class.
And the question in his theme is “How Will You Use Your Gift?”
We all love gifts.
We love to receive gifts, and we like to give gifts.
And where do we get that from?
The originator of gift-giving, Jehovah God.
He loves to give ‘good gifts and perfect presents.’
And of Jehovah’s gifts, Insight on the Scriptures says
that ‘Assignments of service in God’s organization
‘are really gifts from Jehovah.
‘Those favored with assignments of service by God’s undeserved kindness
are also called “gifts in men”’.
And we can say gifts in women.
And what do they do with this gift?
‘They’re given to the congregation in order that its members individually
might be built up and attain maturity.’
Gilead School is a precious gift from Jehovah
that has enabled 141 classes to do just that
—build up their brothers and their sisters.
The question is, How will the 141st class use this gift?
Let’s find out.
We have four students that we would like to interview
—two single students and a married couple.
First of all, we have Anita Schumi, who is originally from Austria.
We have Ben Pritchard, from Britain,
and a married couple from the United States,
Niell and Deanne Ryan.
In preparing for this interview, it was very heartwarming to learn
that all four of you received a precious gift from Jehovah
and that is being raised in the truth by God-fearing parents
who instilled a love for Jehovah in your hearts
as well as the pioneer spirit.
So eventually all four of you pioneered.
But here’s a question.
We’ll start out with Anita.
What other gifts of service did you receive from Jehovah
before coming to Gilead?
After my schooling, I moved to France and started pioneering.
There were many Tamil-speaking people in the territory,
so I started learning that language and finally moved to Asia.
Then I was invited to serve in the Tamil field
in Germany as a special pioneer.
And after seven wonderful years there,
I was sent back to Asia, where I now am.
Thank you. And, Ben.
A few years after attending
the Ministerial Training School in England,
I was assigned to Burkina Faso, in West Africa,
serving as a missionary, which is where I’ve been serving up until now.
A big challenge for me was learning
the local African language called Mooré.
And after about a year or so of learning and struggling with the language,
I wasn’t really up to reading the paragraphs
or saying a prayer at the book study.
However, it was at that point that I was invited
to take up the traveling work on a circuit in that very language.
In fact, the first full-length talk that I did in the language
was the needs of the circuit at the circuit assembly.
But with holy spirit and a lot of patience on the part of the brothers,
I was able gradually to get to grasp with the challenge.
Jehovah certainly helped you.
Deanne.
Well, after Niell and I were married,
I went and joined him at Brooklyn Bethel,
and we served there together until 2004.
And then we left to assist family, and we pioneered together.
And then in 2009, our circumstances opened up
and we reapplied for Bethel service.
However, we were encouraged at that time
to pursue other theocratic goals.
So that’s when we started considering serving in a foreign country.
And I must say, we were definitely nervous
about going to another country—foreign.
But we prayed about it, and we did research.
And then we wrote 31 letters to various branches
to see if we could serve in their territory,
and we got invited to serve in Ghana.
So we’ve been at the Ghana branch for almost six years now.
And although we were very hesitant at first,
we’re very glad we moved, and we enjoy that assignment very much.
So, no doubt, serving in a foreign country has so many blessings,
so many rewards, but also it has its challenges.
So how have the local brothers and sisters
become “gifts in men” and gifts in women to help you to adjust?
Anita.
Not only did they give me a lot of practical help to settle in,
they also patiently explained to me the meaning
and the feelings behind cultural habits.
And that’s worth so much in order to adapt.
So despite cultural differences initially,
many brothers —they took me in like family.
I realized how much more I have in common with my brothers in other countries
than with people from my birth country or my language or my color
who don’t love Jehovah.
Listening to my brothers express their love for the same Father I love
and seeing how he blesses them and helps them
as he helps me, I feel very close to them.
I feel at home.
We have a family wherever we go in the world.
We don’t only call each other
brothers and sisters, we really are.
What a gift!
And through their marvelous example —many in this family—
they taught me valuable lessons in endurance,
patience, devotion, hospitality, and so on.
They trained me so that I could even come here.
They are a very precious gift to me.
Thank you for sharing that.
Ben.
My color means that everywhere I go
I stand out as different to everyone else.
Serving in the traveling work in rural areas,
it’s very, very rare to see white people.
So the word that I hear called out to me by the local people
more than anything else —from morning to evening—
is Nasara, which means “white man.”
It means that whatever efforts you make
to learn the local language and the customs,
you’re nearly always viewed as an outsider.
So in contrast, though, the friendship
and support that I enjoy from the local brothers
really is a gift.
Being taken in by the brothers, eating with them,
living with their family, and being treated by them as family,
whilst outsiders look on
—perhaps surprised— that really is special.
A favorite moment for me in service is when an African brother
working with me will introduce me as “my brother.”
Sometimes the reaction from the householder is:
“How can he be your brother? He’s white and you’re black.”
Then often the reaction will come from the brother,
“Well, he’s more my brother than anyone born in the same village as me.”
So when you hear that kind of statement, in those circumstances, it’s really a gift.
But more than that, I think that the support and friendship
from so many brothers in my assignment has helped me
to keep a positive attitude.
And I can really say it’s because of that, it’s because of them,
that I qualify to be here
and to enjoy this undeserved privilege of Gilead.
Because of that, I really feel the responsibility
now to go back, get to work, and to pass onto others
the gift that I’ve been privileged to receive here.
Thank you.
And going to Ghana, what about you, Deanne?
What do you think about the local brothers and sisters?
How have they helped you?
I really appreciate the kindness of the brothers and sisters in Ghana.
They go out of their way to help you.
And I remember when I was new to the country,
going out in the ministry, I met so many interested people,
but I worried how was I ever going to find them again
because the territory oftentimes doesn’t have
street names and house numbers.
So I would just write a description of where I was.
And the brothers and sisters were so kind.
They wouldn’t just tell me how to get back to my return visits,
they always physically took me there
even if they had to go out of their way to do it.
And that kindness has been repeated in so many different ways.
I don’t have time to relate, but it helped me not only to adjust
to my assignment in Ghana but also to stay in it,
and even to be able to come here to Gilead today.
And, Niell.
I’d say being in a new assignment away from family and friends,
you definitely have your ups and downs, especially in the beginning.
But that scripture at Colossians 4:11
helps me to see that my brothers can be “a source of great comfort”
or “strengthening aid” to us.
And we definitely felt that with the Bethelites
there in Ghana and the congregation.
They were like a second family to us.
They invited us over for hospitality right away.
If you looked a little down, you got an extra warm smile
or a hug or an arm around you.
They just accepted us as a part of their family.
I can definitely say that’s one of the main reasons
why we’re still in that assignment.
And we really appreciate this gift of the worldwide brotherhood.
It’s really helped us to be where we are today
—tasting of this undeserved kindness.
So a recurring theme that “gifts in men,”
gifts in women, really has helped you to adjust.
And I’m sure you will use that going forward.
Now, you have received many gifts of training at Gilead
thus far over the last couple of months.
Is there a specific gem or a gift that has really touched your heart
that you would like to share with us?
So often I was made aware of how little I measure up
to Jehovah’s image in my personality.
And that awareness is good for developing more humility,
but it can be also quite discouraging at times.
It’s a struggle to come to that sound mind,
that balance between I’m not always an outstanding success,
but I’m not a constant failure either.
The course was a marvelous training
in how not to concentrate on my strong points only
—that’s unrealistic—
but also how not to concentrate on my weaknesses only
and then despair, because that’s unhealthy as well.
And that ignores Jehovah’s mercy and his patience with us.
And he showers us with his affections
and wants us to feel joy in serving him.
So I will continue to pray for Jehovah’s help in this regard,
because I want Jehovah to feel more joy
when he watches my thinking and my feelings
become more balanced, more pleasing to him.
Very well expressed. We’ll remember that.
And, Ben.
For me, one point was regarding Abraham
who after having as good as offered up Isaac,
never understood for the rest of his life
the reason why Jehovah asked him
to do that specific thing as a test of his faith.
However, he didn’t then go on to negotiate with Jehovah
—either beforehand or after—
as he had done 25 years before with Lot and Sodom and Gomorrah.
He didn’t obsess with the questions:
“Why? Why would Jehovah allow me
“to go through such a traumatic experience?
Why? Why? Why?”
He just got on with faithfully serving Jehovah.
And in the resurrection he, unlike us who understand the reason why,
he will come to understand the reason why and will feel privileged.
So the application that was made—
The question was asked of us, “What is your personal Isaac?”
Perhaps a situation in this system of things
that we’ll never be rid of,
or a change of assignment, a reassignment,
another difficult change in our service.
Rather than obsessing with the questions:
“Why? Why me? Why did this happen?”
Like Abraham, we should just carry on serving Jehovah loyally.
Deanne.
I really was affected by the lessons in the “Growing Spiritually” section.
In one of them, the instructor used a vivid illustration about—
He said we shouldn’t let the 20 weeks of Gilead pass by
without lancing the boil and cleaning out the pus.
Well, as a nurse, I instantly got a mental image of that
because if someone does have chronic boils
and they don’t do anything about it, it could make them very sick.
So I thought in a spiritual way if through my in-depth study of the Bible
I found negative qualities in my personality
and I did nothing about it,
that spiritually that could infect my whole personality
and make me spiritually sick
and then not as useful to Jehovah as I could be.
And, Niell, a gem for you.
Well, time and again, it was sounded down into our minds
and deep within our hearts that one remains useful to Jehovah
as long as one remains humble.
So I thought about that, that if I begin to think
that it’s all about me or if it’s about my wife, Deanne,
and really forget the much larger picture
—it’s about Jehovah’s sovereignty, his name, the disciple-making work,
and loving and assisting the brothers we’ve been sent there to assist.
Well, then we begin to focus on ourselves,
and we damage our relationship with Jehovah,
and we damage those that we’ve been sent to help.
So throughout the course, Scriptural warnings were studied
on King Uzziah, King Saul, and Korah
who started out as humble but they went—
they lost that humility and became very prideful.
They forgot the place that Jehovah had put them in.
And I won’t forget a point made by a Governing Body member
that was relating what Brother Knorr
used to say to the students —to Gilead students.
He said that if you leave Gilead with a bigger head than a bigger heart,
then we have failed you.
And so we want to be very willing to be humble
and do whatever Jehovah has asked of us.
So how do you plan on using this beautiful gift of Gilead training?
Anita.
The whole Gilead experience
has stressed how much Jehovah cares for each of our brothers.
For example, at 1 Kings 10:9,
we learned that Jehovah put Solomon in place as king,
not for Solomon’s glory,
but he was used as a channel for Jehovah to show His love for Israel.
So likewise, Jehovah gave us this training here,
not for our glory, but for our brothers.
He equipped us to show
how to take care of our brothers in a more loving way,
to transmit the gifts and Jehovah’s love to them,
make them feel his care, and strengthen their attachment to Jehovah.
So I am eager to return and try my best to do just that
—as a little thank you to Jehovah for the marvelous time here
but also as a thank you to my brothers back home to whom I owe so much.
Very good.
And, Ben.
It’s true that Gilead has given us knowledge,
but Gilead isn’t about knowing things.
So I want to keep in mind what Ephesians 3:19 says,
‘The love of the Christ surpasses knowledge.’
Which means taking knowledge and then transforming it
into experience by imitation
—imitation of Christ.
So I hope to be a better imitator of Christ
as I go back and serve with the brothers.
But that means not just imitating Jesus in my actions
but also coming to have the same feelings
that Jesus has about things and about people.
In addition to that, Jehovah really has used—
has given me so many “gifts in men” here at Gilead
that have helped me to increase my love for him
but also to have a real deep affection
for the organization that he’s using.
So as I go back, I want to be a factor in helping others
to come to see how much Jehovah loves them
and see how wonderful the organization that he is using really is.
And last, we’ll hear from the Ryans.
Deanne.
At Psalm 78:5-7,
it speaks of parents making known Jehovah’s reminders
to the next generation so they can put their confidence in Jehovah.
And I’d like to do something similar when I go back to Ghana,
especially with the young ones,
to share the many spiritual gems that I’ve been given
so that they can more fully put their confidence in Jehovah.
So I’d like to do that whenever I see them at the meetings,
or talking before and after, working with them in the ministry,
when they come over to visit me in my room at Bethel,
really, whatever opportunity I have to share those gems with them.
And 2 Timothy 2:2 reminds me
that after we’ve received this beautiful training,
we have responsibility, and that is, in turn,
to teach or train others.
So as I go back to my assignment,
I hope to keep learning from the brothers and sisters there
but also to share these gems and gifts with them.
Not as a heavy downpour that drowns our brothers and sisters,
but as a gentle shower that encourages them.
For example, I’d love to work with the young ones
and share the experience of young Samuel when he went to the tabernacle
and how he served Jehovah faithfully
despite the wicked influence of Eli’s two sons,
and that they too can be faithful
despite the negative influence of this world around them.
If we share these gifts with the brothers and sisters
—like a gentle shower—
we’ll show that we haven’t missed the purpose of this Gilead training,
and that is to encourage and strengthen the brothers
and bring honor and glory to Jehovah.
We’d like to thank all four of you for your heartfelt comments,
and you really expressed yourselves so well,
and you represented the rest of your class so well.
So with Jehovah’s help, we know that you will use
all the gifts that have been given to you
to be a gift to all those in your assignments.
Thank you.
Thank you very much Brother Curzan.
That was very refreshing.
Appreciate them sharing those thoughts.
Now we invite you to stand
and we’ll sing this beloved song, number 29,
“Walking in Integrity,” song number 29.
